prose: Proof that can be checked is different in kind from proof that is claimed. Its value depends on operators caring about the difference — a manifest nobody verifies buys the same trust as the assertion, at more cost.

tests.title: Test does a published manifest increase operator trust

title: An instance can deliver to the central inbox on what it already holds, with its provenance intact
prose: The feasibility half, separate from consent. If reaching the inbox needs a new credential the operator has to obtain, the cost lands exactly where the fleet is widest; and if items lose their attribution in the merge, the inbox holds a pile nobody can trace back to the instance that produced it.

tests.title: A fleet instance reaches the inbox with no new credential, and its provenance survives the trip

title: An isolated worktree per firing prevents state leakage without adding meaningful setup cost
prose:
Feasibility/cost assumption: creating a fresh worktree per firing actually stops one firing's edits (including an edit to the automation scripts) from being inherited by the next firing's checkout, and the setup/teardown cost of doing this every firing is small enough not to matter against how often firings run.

This is answerable from the repository — time how long a worktree create/remove cycle takes against the shared-checkout pattern it replaces, and confirm a worktree genuinely isolates an in-progress edit. No customer interview is needed; a human or an attended pass with repo sight should confirm before treating this as tested.

tests.title: Two firings in per-firing worktrees leave the shared checkout clean with the residue waiver switched off

title: An observation can be recorded without becoming a verdict that clears a gate
prose: The split holds only if the recorded exit code stays inert — written to the instrument log, never to Results, never moving a status. If anything downstream reads an exit code as evidence, the runner has quietly granted itself the authority the split exists to withhold.

tests.title: Check that a recorded exit code cannot clear a gate or masquerade as a result

title: An operator consents to being asked, and finds the questions worth their time
prose: An agent withholding its answer to test its operator is doing something the operator has to have agreed to. An operator in a hurry experiences it as being quizzed by their own tooling — so consent and frequency both have to be theirs, and the questions have to be ones they are glad were asked.

tests.title: Withhold the agent's answer on ten forks and measure how often the operator diverges

title: An operator facing a queue of drafts keeps reading them rather than approving in bulk
prose: Bulk approval is indistinguishable from automation while feeling like oversight — which is worse than automating openly, because the operator now believes they understand a tree they skimmed. Whether attention holds across forty drafts is the whole question.

tests.title: Queue forty drafts for approval and record how long the operator spends on each

title: An operator handed a refusals section acts on it instead of learning to skip it
prose:
**Desirability.** The solution assumes the missing thing is information. It may be that the information was always available and the operator's problem is attention, in which case adding a section at the top of a report changes where the failure sits without removing it.

Stated so it can be false: an operator who receives, every morning, a list of everything the night could not do, stops reading that list. There is a specific mechanism for this and the tree already names it one bucket over — "Three gates fired correctly in one session and every one of them read as noise first" records three correct signals being read as noise on first sight. A refusals section is a signal of exactly that shape: usually the same four entries, usually not urgent, always at the top. The second week is when it stops working, not the first, which is why a one-morning trial would confirm it falsely.

There is a sharper version of the doubt. The five recorded sessions were denied the same four tools every time. A section reporting that would have been byte-identical five mornings running. A signal that never changes is one an operator is right to stop reading — so if this is built at all it may have to report only *new* refusals, or refusals whose blocked work has grown, and that is a different solution from the one the parent node proposes.

Where it could be true: the denials in the record were not merely unread, they were invisible. The operator had no artefact to skim past. There is a real difference between ignoring a line and never being shown one, and the first two weeks of the first version are the only place to find out which of the two this was.

The feasibility half of this solution is not in doubt and is not what this assumption is about: a denied call arrives at the run as an error it can see and count, which is how the transcript adapter came to hold all fifteen of them in the first place.

tests.title: Run the refusals section for two weeks and count the mornings it changes anything

title: An operator notified at every block keeps acting on the notifications rather than tuning them out
prose: Immediate announcement puts the operator on call. A person messaged every time an unattended run needs them has not been freed by automation, and the failure mode is not refusal but attrition — week two's notifications quietly going unread.

tests.title: Send one notification per block for two weeks and count how many the operator acts on

title: An operator shown the evidence will accept an elimination they initially disagreed with
prose: Elimination-by-evidence produces a shrinking consideration set without crowning anything, which fits the ruleset. It depends on the evidence being persuasive against a prior — if operators re-add what the tournament removed, the rounds have done nothing but add ceremony.

tests.title: Would an operator accept an elimination they initially disagreed with once shown the evidence

title: An operator shown the line that was actually written notices when it is wrong
prose: Returning the content rather than a confirmation puts the error in front of the person. It only helps if they read it — an echo scrolled past is the same as a confirmation, and the destroyed note is still destroyed.

tests.title: Does an operator notice a bad write when the tool echoes the line back

title: An operator who must move the window by hand will actually move it more than once
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** An operator handed a config key that selects which slice of the backlog their firings are shown will amend it repeatedly over the life of a tree, rather than setting it once and leaving it.

**Risk category: desirability, shading into usability.** It is a claim about what a person will do with a control, and no amount of reading the code settles it.

**Why it is the riskiest thing this candidate rests on.** The entire coverage benefit is downstream of the amending. Set once and forgotten, this candidate is bit-for-bit today's defect with a new owner — the same 25 items every firing, forever, now by the operator's own configuration. So the candidate is not "a way to advance the window"; it is a bet that a person will advance it, and the bet is the whole thing.

**Prior evidence that cuts against it, which is why the bet is worth naming rather than assuming.** This tree carries 51 outstanding asks, every one of them a question put to the operator with a ready-made command that would answer it, and all 51 have gone unanswered long enough that none carries a recorded age. It also carries a standing hold on a sibling branch that nine consecutive firings have logged and nobody has resolved. The observed base rate for "the operator will perform a small recurring maintenance act on this vault" is, on the record available, low. That is not proof — none of those asks is this ask, and an operator may well treat steering their own attention differently from answering a queue of test verdicts — but a candidate whose value rests entirely on operator follow-through should be read against it.

**What settles it.** Watching, not asking. A stated intention to amend a config key is close to free to give and is not the measurement.

**What a supported verdict would still leave open.** Nothing about whether the window mechanism works, which is a separate feasibility question this node does not touch, and nothing about the two sibling candidates, whose value does not depend on anybody doing anything.

tests.title: Count how many times the operator amends discovery.target over eight weeks of git history

title: An operator will actually visit a queue that never chases them
prose: Nothing pursues the operator, which is the point and the risk. The node names it: if the ask rate exceeds the visit rate for long, the queue becomes furniture — a monument to blocked work where there used to be a small surprise.

tests.title: Build the queue from asks already outstanding and see whether the operator empties it once

title: An operator will adopt an outside-sourced candidate into their real consideration set
prose: Seeding from other products and non-software processes widens the set beyond what the current context could produce. Width is only valuable if the imported candidates are taken seriously rather than read as interesting and irrelevant.

tests.title: Would an operator adopt an outside-sourced candidate into their consideration set

title: An operator would accept a pass dismissing its own work list by written assertion
prose:
Desirability, and the one that should decide whether this candidate ships at all.

Every other way an item leaves the work list requires the agent to do something checkable — ship code, attach an instrument that fails today, create a node. A disposition removes it by writing a sentence. The party writing that sentence is the party whose budget is spent by the work it dismisses, which is a live incentive rather than a theoretical one.

Stated so it can be false: an operator who is not watching may simply not accept a mechanism whose failure mode is an agent quietly declaring itself finished, however good the audit trail is — in which case the review surface is not a mitigation but a consolation, and the two derivation-based siblings are the only acceptable answers because they cannot be talked into anything.

This is not a question the repository can answer. No spec can tell anyone whether a person would trust the mechanism; the code would pass whatever a person thinks of it.

tests.title: Show five operators a pass's dismissed-work list and ask whether they would have let it stand

title: An unattended pass can resolve the merges this creates without corrupting the tree
prose: Branching moves the problem to whoever merges. If that is an unattended pass, a collision the tree could detect has been swapped for a resolution nobody checks — and the second failure is much harder to notice.

tests.title: Have an unattended pass resolve ten seeded merge conflicts and grade every resolution

title: An unread marker survives to the summary instead of being flattened to zero
prose:
**Feasibility.** Introducing a third return state is easy. Getting it to survive the journey to the number an operator reads is the claim.

Stated so it can be false: every consumer between the search and the summary preserves the distinction between "examined and found nothing" and "could not examine". The pressure runs the other way at each boundary. A caller that wants a count writes `results.length`. A caller that wants to filter writes `results.filter(...)`. Both flatten unread to zero, both are the obvious thing to write, and neither looks wrong at the call site — the harm only appears three layers up, in a total that reads as complete.

This is the same failure the tree already records at the sweep layer: a sweep that cannot read its subject reports a clean result. The unread marker is the fix for it, and the fix has the same shape as the disease, because a marker that is dropped is worse than no marker — it produces the same wrong number with a mechanism in place that everyone believes is protecting them.

Where it could be true: if the search interface never returns a plain collection, and the only way to reach a count is through a call that forces the unread case to be handled, then the flattening path is absent rather than discouraged. That is a stronger property than a convention and it is the version worth building.

Where it stays false no matter what: anywhere a pass reports in prose. This pass wrote several summaries by hand, and a model composing a sentence about what it found has no type system stopping it from saying "no issues" over a subject it could not read. That limit should be stated rather than designed around.

tests.title: Feed every search path a malformed pattern and require the total to say two were unread

title: An up-front authoring session produces axioms the founder still endorses when they matter
prose: **Risk category: desirability.** The register only works if the blank-page authoring session (a) actually gets scheduled and finished, and (b) yields axioms the founder still stands behind when a derivation later leans on them. It could be false: the founder called the acceptable-axiom distinction "really very felt-out," which may mean it is exercised case-by-case and resists being written down in advance — in which case the register fills with shelf axioms that get revised the first time one is load-bearing, and the up-front cost bought nothing over lazy elicitation.

tests.title: Hold one 30-minute axiom-writing session and re-test endorsement a week later

title: Analysis-only firings change decisions rather than producing commentary
prose: **Kind: viability.** A firing licensed to think without clearing buckets is licensed to produce prose nobody acts on — this tree already priced that failure at roughly twenty scheduled passes of commentary. The belief, stated so it can be false: sustained single-branch analysis produces output the operator actually acts on — a re-framing adopted, a solution killed, an assumption re-prioritized — at a rate that justifies spending firings on it instead of on the queue.

tests.title: After three deep-dive firings the operator names a decision their output changed

title: Artifacts are composed incrementally, so there is a line three at which to check
prose: If artifacts are genuinely written whole in a single act, there is no intermediate state to validate and this reduces to a dry-run before submission — a smaller and different idea. Whether the composer can be observed mid-composition is what has to be settled first.

tests.title: Check a partial artifact is rejected at the offending line rather than at submission

title: Asked at the moment the reasoning is still in their head, a collaborator will deposit it — and come back unasked
prose: One question in a surface they already use is the cheapest possible ask. The real test is not the first deposit, which politeness can produce, but a second one nobody prompted — that is the difference between a channel and a favour.

tests.title: Offer the deposit prompt and count who comes back a second time unasked

title: Authors nominate a riskiest assumption other than the one they were already going to test
prose: If nominations reliably match the existing test, the gate has a better name and changes nothing. Whether the nominations are honest is the assumption underneath this whole mechanism, and it needs settling before a gate is built on it.

tests.title: Have authors nominate a riskiest assumption and check it against what they were already testing

title: Authors required to state a differentia produce discriminators, not boilerplate
prose: **Kind: usability.** A gate can require a sentence; it cannot judge one. The belief, stated so it can be false: a pass (or human) forced to write "a solution addressing this and not its sibling is …" at creation time writes real discriminators — statements a reader could use to route evidence between the siblings — rather than title-restating filler that satisfies the gate and discriminates nothing. If the filler rate is high, the gate adds friction without adding distinctness, which is worse than no gate.

tests.title: The operator grades the first ten differentia statements as discriminators or filler

title: Author–judge separation is checkable from the vault's own record
prose:
**Risk category: feasibility.**

The belief, stated so it can be wrong: the vault's own records carry enough provenance — which actor authored a solution's claim, which actor authored the test that judges it, which process recorded the verdict — that the gate-parity rule "the party that authored the claim is not the sole author of its judge" can be evaluated mechanically at gate time, with no human reading history.

Ways it fails, named at birth: authorship may not be recorded at the granularity the rule needs (a session id is not an author when one actor drives every session); History lines are prose, and prose provenance may not parse; and an agent that knows the rule can trivially split its work across two sessions, satisfying the letter of separation while remaining one author — in which case the check measures ceremony, not independence. If any of these holds, the gate-parity solution loses the counterparty substitute it promised and quietly becomes self-grading with extra steps.

This is a question about code and records, not about people: whether a guard can read authorship from what the vault already writes is settled by a spec against the gate, in minutes.

tests.title: Gate refuses a permit when the claim's author is the sole author of its judge

title: Auto-reading a file before write doesn't mask the exact race condition the guard exists to catch
prose: Feasibility/desirability belief: if the file changed between the auto-read and the write actually landing, an invisible auto-read doesn't quietly paper over the same staleness the original guard was built to surface — it could turn a loud, safe failure into a silent, unsafe overwrite.

title: Axiom asks arrive rarely enough to be answered instead of batched into ignorance
prose: **Risk category: viability.** Lazy elicitation trades the up-front session for a stream of small asks. The belief is that the stream is thin enough — a few asks per week, each answerable in a minute — that the operator actually clears it. It could be false: if early theory work fans out (every derivation touching a new corner needs a new axiom), the queue floods, asks age unanswered, and derivations block indefinitely — reproducing exactly the founder's original frustration, an evidence regime the operator cannot feed. The vault's own outstanding-asks machinery shows asks can sit with no answer on record.

tests.title: Seed five axiom asks into the standing queue and count answers within a week

title: Backpressure on instrumenting pushes results to be recorded, rather than just stopping work
prose: If instrumenting is the cheap valuable half and execution is blocked on something structural — a permission, a missing runner, a person's availability — then rationing punishes the part that works to protest the part that does not.

tests.title: Check the instrument allowance holds at the floor while no result has ever been recorded

title: Being told a section was dropped is worth little to a caller with no undo
prose:
Stated deliberately in the direction that would kill its own solution, because that is the honest way round. The belief this solution needs is that a caller told `dropped: ["## History"]` will do something about it. The belief stated here is the opposite, and it is the one with evidence behind it.

An unattended pass has no undo. Told what it destroyed, its only remedy is to reconstruct the content from what it still holds in context. On 2026-08-05 that worked exactly once, and by luck: the pass had read the whole file minutes earlier for an unrelated reason and could restore four `## History` entries verbatim. Had it edited from the tool's own listing — the normal case — the report would have named a loss the caller had no copy of, and the response would have been to write "a section was lost here" into the node, which is a worse artifact than the loss.

So the risk is specific and it is not "nobody reads the report". It is that **reporting converts a silent loss into a documented one without changing the loss rate**, and a team looking at a tool that now names its own damage may reasonably conclude the damage is handled. That would make this solution actively harmful relative to doing nothing, because it spends the attention that the two preventive siblings need.

What would make it false: a caller that can act. If the report carried the dropped content itself, or a git ref to it, restoration becomes mechanical and the objection collapses. That is a different and more expensive solution than the one proposed above, and whether it is the one worth building is the real question this assumption puts to a human.

tests.title: Check every dropped section is reported with enough to restore it

title: Blind parallel ideators produce more distinct candidates than one agent asked for three
prose: Removing the anchoring is the claim. It fails if separate contexts converge anyway — drawn to the same obvious answers by the same evidence — in which case the parallelism costs several times the tokens for the same consideration set.

tests.title: Do blind parallel ideators produce more distinct candidates than one agent asked for three

title: Broken inherited trees are common enough, and the check cheap enough, to pay for it every run
prose: A preflight build check is a tax on every run to catch a rare state. It is worth it only if broken starts actually occur at some rate and the check stays fast enough not to matter.

tests.title: Time the build check against how often a run would actually have found a broken tree

title: Buyers have been burned by lock-in recently enough to pay for portability
prose: Portability may be a real advantage nobody pays for, which is a different failure from not having one. The question is whether buyers have a live memory of losing something to a shutdown — because they do not price this until they need it, and by then they are not shopping.

tests.title: Ask ten buyers what happened the last time a tool they relied on shut down

title: Buyers treat refusals as trustworthiness rather than as the product being worse
prose: The whole position rests on buyers punishing overclaiming. They may instead prefer the tool that says yes, and experience every refusal as a missing feature — which is the desirability assumption under the entire strategy, and it is untested.

tests.title: Pitch the refusals to ten prospects and count who treats them as a feature

title: Buyers value the design of a test, not just the running of it
prose: Pricing per tested assumption assumes the buyer is paying for the whole unit. If they see design as the cheap part and execution as the expensive part, the price is attached to the half they do not value and the unit is wrong.

tests.title: Ask ten buyers to split a test's price between designing it and running it

title: Charting cost can be estimated well enough in advance to inform the choice
prose: The node names the trap: a bad estimate is worse than none, because it will be wrong in the direction that justifies whatever was already wanted, and there is no obvious way to calibrate it before the fact.

tests.title: Estimate charting cost for three past goals and check the estimates against what happened

title: Checks over a hand-built vault surface findings its owner did not already know
prose: Conceding the generation makes for an easier sale and possibly a worse business. It also does not answer the opportunity as written — it makes the question go away rather than answering it — so the checks have to earn their place by finding real things their owner had missed.

tests.title: Run the checks over three hand-built vaults and count findings the owner did not already know

title: Claims on this tree go stale mostly because a new record arrived, not for reasons ingest never sees
prose:
**Efficacy belief, and the one that decides whether this candidate is worth building at all:** when a measured claim on this tree stops being true, the thing that made it stop is usually a record the vault subsequently ingested.

It held for the originating instance — the 2026-08-16 census was falsified by a transcript captured the next day, and an ingest-time tripwire would have named it within the hour. One instance is not the rate.

**Why it might be false.** Plenty of claims here rest on things ingest never touches: a config value changed by hand (the `product.repos` line, which invalidated a bar's stated remedy without producing any record), a shipped code change, a grant table edited outside the vault, or a claim that was simply wrong the day it was written and never had a falsifying record to wait for. If those are the majority, a tripwire at ingest catches the tail and the operator still cannot read an unflagged claim as current — which leaves this candidate solving the visible instance and not the need.

Note what this assumption is *not* about: whether the check can be built (that is the sibling assumption beside it) or whether an operator would act on the flag. It is about the population of stale claims, and it is answerable only by looking at claims that have already gone stale here.

tests.title: Classify 12 already-falsified claims from this vault's git history by what falsified each

title: Class-level ranking matches how the founder actually triages a live backlog
prose: **Risk category: desirability.** The directive asks for class-level rank verbs, but asking for a verb and reaching for it under load are different facts. This belief is that, given a real triage moment over this tree's own backlog, the founder ranks *classes* — and the class boundaries the tree can draw are the ones they mean. It could be false two ways: they may fall back to per-node judgements the moment a class contains one node they feel differently about, or the classes the tree can express (today: the category buckets) may not be the classes in their head.

tests.title: Run one live triage offering only class-rank verbs and watch for per-node fallback

title: Conditions that expire are more often genuinely slow than never going to be true
prose:
**Risk category: viability.**

The belief, stated so it could turn out false: among the waits that actually expire in this loop, the ones that would have succeeded given more time outnumber the ones that were never going to succeed.

**Why the direction matters more than the mechanism.** Automatic escalation is patience made cheap. If most expiries are genuinely-slow subjects, cheap patience is exactly right and the candidate turns a 300s dead end into a 600s success. If most expiries are never-true conditions — a typo in the grep, a file the subject never writes, a job that died at second three — then the candidate spends up to 2100s of unattended wall clock where today it spends 300s, and it makes the problem it was built for strictly worse. The candidate's own prose names this as the thing that decides it; this node is that thing.

**What makes it genuinely uncertain rather than obvious.** The one recorded instance cuts against the candidate: in `TRANSCRIPT:8910f58f` the condition was `grep -q "Test Files" /tmp/suite-branch.txt`, and it failed five times over roughly twenty minutes. Whether the suite was slow or the redirect never landed is not recoverable from the record — which is itself the parent opportunity's point — so even the one case on hand does not settle the direction.

**Not the only belief beneath that solution.** It also assumes two different waits on the same condition string can safely be treated as one wait retried. That identity question is named in the solution's prose and is not carried here.

tests.title: Count the recorded expiries that later succeeded against those whose condition could never have become true

title: Conflicts are rare and contested enough that human-only resolution does not flood the operator
prose: Most conflicts in an append-only Markdown vault are mechanical and safely resolved. A rule treating all of them as human-only sends a great deal of trivia to the operator — and an operator sent enough trivia stops reading any of it.

tests.title: Count how many vault conflicts are mechanical, to see what a human-only rule would actually cost

title: Corroboration can be recorded without asserting a new need
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** The whole value of this candidate rests on corroboration being a *lighter* act than creating a node — an item leaves the queue, a count rises, and nothing new is claimed. If filing corroboration turns out to mint a node, mutate the target's evidence rung, or otherwise move a gate, then it is node creation wearing a cheaper name, and an unattended pass filing 76 items would have quietly raised the believability of four opportunities without a single new observation behind it.

The rung is the specific danger. Seventy-six transcript records attached to one node must not make that node more believable than one record does: they are one channel observed repeatedly, not independent sources, and the ladder's whole point is that repetition is not corroboration.

**What would make it false.** Filing corroboration changing anything on the target beyond a count and a recorded id — in particular its evidence rung.

tests.title: Filing corroboration clears the item and moves no rung

title: Credentialed steps sit late in a run rather than upstream of everything else
prose: The classification is right and useless if the secret is needed early. Whether credentialed work is terminal or load-bearing is answerable from real run journals before any of this is built.

tests.title: Classify the steps of ten past runs as credentialed or not, and see how much work sits upstream

title: Dated claims here are spread across enough ages that an expiry label separates some from others
prose:
**Feasibility belief about this vault's own shape, not about the mechanism:** the dated measured claims on this tree are spread across enough different ages that marking the old ones actually partitions them.

A label is only information if it discriminates. If nearly every dated claim here is old — and this tree is dense with first-party observations from single passes that nothing will ever re-take — then at any plausible shelf life almost everything reads "not measured since", and a reader learns exactly what they knew before opening the node. That is the unlabelled state with more words, which this candidate's own body names as its risk.

The failure runs both ways and both are worth stating, because they argue for opposite shelf lives and one of them is the trap. **Too much expired** and the label is noise. **Too little** and it never fires, so the mechanism costs a field and buys nothing — and this is the trap, because a label that never fires looks exactly like a label that is working. Neither reading can be taken from the mechanism; both are properties of the corpus, and both are countable today over the vault as it stands.

What this assumption deliberately does not cover: whether an operator changes what they do on seeing the label. That is a different belief and a person is the only measurement of it.

tests.title: Count this vault's dated claims by age and require the expired share to fall between 10 and 70 percent

title: Decisions taken on a stated assumption are mostly accepted, and the review is short enough to happen
prose: Authority is taken by the run and returned at review, so the arrangement collapses if the review does not happen. Both halves matter: enough decisions accepted that reversal is rare, and a review small enough to fit one sitting rather than being deferred indefinitely.

tests.title: Show the operator ten forks already taken and count the reversals and the minutes

title: Declaring the operator's real resources changes which work comes first
prose: The manifest is only worth its filling-in if it moves the order. If the top priorities are the same before and after an honest declaration, then the ranking was never actually conditioned on resources and the manifest is a form with no consequence.

tests.title: Hand-fill the manifest and count how many of the top five priorities move

title: Denying Write on automation-script paths still lets the build agent finish every task it's actually asked to do
prose:
Feasibility assumption: revoking Write on the automation-script paths closes the hole (a build session editing the scripts that govern every future firing) without also blocking legitimate build work that never needs to touch those paths. If normal build tasks occasionally DO need to edit automation scripts (e.g. shipping a fix to the loop itself), a blanket deny either breaks that class of work or has to be special-cased, which reopens the same hole through the exception.

This is answerable from the repository: which build tasks, if any, have historically needed to write to the automation-script paths, and whether the permission boundary can be drawn to exclude only those. No customer interview is needed — a human or an attended pass with repo sight should confirm before treating this as tested.

tests.title: The build-pass invocation denies Write on its own automation-script paths while still granting Write elsewhere

title: Discovery done because the budget exists is as useful as discovery done because someone chose it
prose: Reserving compute makes discovery happen regardless of anyone's appetite for it. The risk is that unchosen work is unmotivated work — reserved passes that produce output nobody wanted would make the budget a way of spending money on schedule.

tests.title: Three reserved discovery passes rated for usefulness

title: Displaying an item is a sufficient signal to advance the window, with no disposition state at all
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Sorting by "when was this last shown to a firing" is enough on its own to make a second firing see members the first was not — without anyone deciding what counts as handled, and without any item ever leaving the queue.

**Risk category: feasibility.** It is a claim about whether the mechanism works, not about whether anyone wants it.

**How it could turn out false.** The stamp is written when a list is *served*, and a list is served every time `ost_next_work` is called. A single firing calls it repeatedly — the maintenance loop is explicitly "re-call `ost_ingest_inbox`, then `ost_next_work`, and repeat" — so within one pass the first call stamps the head, the second call is shown the next 25, the third the next, and by the end of a long pass the ordering has churned through a large slice of the queue without any of it being worked. The next firing then starts wherever the previous one's last confirmation call happened to leave off, which is not the same as "where the previous firing stopped paying attention". If that is how it behaves, the mechanism advances the window faster than it advances the reading, and the guarantee it was bought for — everything is eventually *seen* — degrades into everything is eventually *scrolled past*.

**What settles it.** Two calls that differ only in being the second, over a queue larger than the cap, must return disjoint or near-disjoint members; and the stamp must distinguish a firing from a call, or the paragraph above is what happens.

**What a green here would still leave open.** Nothing about whether rotation is the right policy, and nothing about whether an operator would rather choose the slice themselves. Feasibility only.

tests.title: A second computeNextWork call on an unchanged vault returns capped-list members the first did not

title: Drift is auditable after the fact from the pass records alone
prose: The audit half only works if each pass carries the outcome it ran against, in its own record. If distinguishing two passes requires consulting the vault's current outcome, then the record cannot show what changed — which is precisely the case where it is needed.

tests.title: Every pass records the outcome text it ran against, and a changed outcome is visible as a change

title: Dropping the envelope test admits the product's own refusals without admitting ordinary command failures
prose:
**Risk category: feasibility.**

The belief, stated so it could turn out false: with `GUARD_MARKER` removed, `splitRefusal` alone is a good enough discriminator — it keeps the refusals an `ost_*` tool issues (which name a permitted form and arrive with no `<tool_use_error>` wrapper) and still drops a command that merely exited non-zero (which names no permitted form, wrapper or not).

**How it could be false.** `splitRefusal`'s remedy cues are four ordinary English words — `use`, `must`, `instead`, `try`. A failing command's own output can contain any of them within the last 400 characters and would then be read as advice. The module's docstring records exactly this going wrong once, on a `String to replace not found in file.` message whose quoted payload contained the word "must"; the end-anchoring rule was added to fix that instance. Whether that rule generalises past the instance that prompted it is precisely what is unknown, and it is the whole bet of the candidate above.

**Why this is the sharpest of the risks here.** The candidate's other risks are cheap to live with. This one decides whether the change is an improvement or a regression, because a ledger that fills with non-corrections fails in the same direction the ledger was built to fix — becoming long enough that nobody reads it.

**What settling it does not settle.** Nothing about desirability. A correctly-populated ledger is not evidence that carrying these corrections forward changes what a later session writes, which is a separate belief and would need its own test.

tests.title: An unwrapped MCP refusal is extracted as a correction while a non-zero exit still is not

title: Editor tooling can auto-read a file transparently before a first Write Edit without weakening the guard's protection against blind overwrites
prose: The guard exists to stop a session from overwriting content it never looked at. Auto-reading on the session's behalf only preserves that protection if the auto-read genuinely happens first and its content is what the session's subsequent edit is computed against — not a stale or partial read inserted after the edit was already planned. If the harness can't guarantee ordering, "auto-read" could silently become "assume it's fine," which is the failure mode the guard was built to prevent.

tests.title: Have someone with the editor-tool source open confirm auto-read can run strictly before the edit it guards

title: Empty and undefined writes actually landed in the vault histories
prose: Putting the guard at the vault rather than the call catches whatever produced the bad content. Whether it is worth having is answered by the histories: a sweep either finds writes that landed as undefined or shows the class is theoretical.

tests.title: Sweep both vault histories for writes that landed as undefined or empty

title: Enough distinct files get hand-excluded that declaring them once beats retyping
prose: A committed list pays for itself across repetition and breadth. At one or two distinct files it is over-engineering — the retyping was cheap and the list is a second place for the truth to live.

tests.title: Count the distinct test files ever hand-excluded across the captured sessions

title: Enough failed calls are shape errors that schema validation catches a real share of them
prose: Checking against the published schema is free in the sense that the schema exists. It only prevents damage if the failures are shape errors — a call that is well-formed and means the wrong thing passes validation and destroys the note anyway.

tests.title: Sort a day of real failed calls into shape errors and meaning errors

title: Enough of a run's remaining work sits independent of whatever blocked it
prose: Carrying on requires something to carry on with. If most of the run is downstream of the blocked step there is nothing independent left, and the operator now hears about the block later than they would have.

tests.title: Take ten past blocked runs and measure how much work sat independent of the block

title: Enough of the tree is already ordered by a recorded human decision to rank from
prose: The agent never authors a priority, so coverage is everything. If only a fraction of rows trace to a recorded decision, most of the tree stays unranked — which is honest, and may be too little ordering to be useful.

tests.title: Count how much of the tree a recorded decision could actually order

title: Enough open assumptions in the tree could be moved by public information to be worth the channel
prose: Spending lookups only against stated questions makes every finding arrive attached to what it bears on. Its limit is structural: it can only ask what the tree already knows to ask, so a vault whose blind spots are its problem gets efficient answers to the wrong questions.

tests.title: Count how many open assumptions in this tree could be moved by anything public at all

title: Enough recorded steps are side-effect-free to be safely replayable by a fixed rule
prose: Making the record executable answers 'does this still fail?' directly. It requires deciding safety mechanically — a replay that reruns something with side effects is worse than an unanswerable question, and case-by-case judgement is not available here.

tests.title: Count how many recorded steps are safely replayable at all

title: Enough refusal classes are safe to absorb that removing the occasion is worth doing
prose: Some refusals are load-bearing safety, and accommodating the wrong form is how a guardrail becomes decorative. Which classes are safe to absorb is a human's call — and there have to be enough of them, covering enough of the volume, to justify the work.

tests.title: Sort the top refusal classes into safe-to-absorb and load-bearing, and count each

title: Enough timed-check runs happen somewhere isolation can be guaranteed
prose: Removing the contention instead of tolerating it makes the check meaningful where it can fail. If most runs happen where isolation cannot be promised, the check is advisory almost everywhere — and advisory numbers get scrolled past for months while the regression they watched for arrives.

tests.title: Count how many timed checks would run somewhere that cannot guarantee isolation

title: Enough true, useful, non-need evidence is being stranded to justify a layer of its own
prose: A new node type earns its complexity only if there is a real population for it. If the stranded items are few, or if they turn out to be opportunities written badly rather than genuinely need-shaped nothing, then the layer is machinery for a case that barely occurs.

tests.title: Count stranded evidence items across both vaults that only a Context node could home

title: Error classes can be grouped so the counter fires on the second real repeat and changes behaviour
prose: Two zsh failures with different messages are the same class, and two identical messages from different causes are not. Get that wrong and the counter either never fires or cries wolf — and a wolf-crying counter is quickly ignored. Firing is also not enough: the session has to change approach.

tests.title: Apply the escalating message to the five-failure session and check where it would have fired
Replay the five-failure and three-failure sessions through the class counter and require it to fire by the second occurrence in both
Show the escalated message to five fresh sessions facing the same failure and count which change approach

title: Every ask in the standing queue carries the date it was asked, whichever surface filed it
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false:** every entry that reaches the standing queue carries a real `askedAt`, no matter which surface put it there — a mid-pass flag, a human's CLI classification, or a test created humans-required in the first place.

**Why it is the load-bearing belief under this solution.** The parent node's own argument is that age is what separates a queue from a second inbox: "An ask that has been outstanding for eleven days is a different object from one filed an hour ago, and only the queue can tell the operator that." If an entry can arrive with no date, the queue degrades into exactly the undated backlog the node says it is not — and it does so silently, because a null age still renders as a row.

**Why this pass thinks it is currently false, from first-party repository reading (2026-08-28).** Membership and age come from two different places. `src/ost/pending-asks.ts` admits an entry when *either* the test's lane says a person is what it waits on *or* an ask is on the ledger — but `askedAt` and `ageDays` are read from the ledger alone, and are `null` when there is none. `src/ost/lanes.ts` calls `appendAsk` from the lane-setting path. So a test that acquires the humans-required lane at creation, rather than by being flagged or classified later, enters the queue through the lane branch and never touches the ledger.

The production reading matches: this pass's own `ost_next_work` reports 52 outstanding asks and says all 52 "predate ask tracking and have no recorded age." Not most — every one. A partial legacy migration would leave a mixture; a creation path that never files leaves exactly this. One entry, "A human re-judges the first twelve extent flags against Torres's test", is a test this vault's own sweeps created with `humansRequired` supplied at creation, and it carries `lane: humans-required` with `askedAt: null`.

**The consequence worth naming.** The one surface that creates humans-required tests in volume — an unattended pass calling `ost_create_node` — is also the surface on which `ost_flag_humans_required` is withheld. So the path that files asks is closed to the actor that generates them, and the path that is open to it does not file. That is why the count is 52 of 52 rather than a few stragglers.

**What would make this belief true after all, and would refute the reading above:** creation could file an ask somewhere this pass did not read (`src/mcp/server.ts` was not opened), or the 52 could genuinely all predate the ledger. Either would show up as a green on the test beneath this node.

**Class:** feasibility. It is a question about what this codebase does, answerable by a spec rather than by anyone's afternoon — which is why it is instrumented rather than sent to the humans-required lane.

_Source: first-party `ost_read_repo` reads this pass of `src/ost/pending-asks.ts`, `src/ost/lanes.ts`, `test/ost/pending-ask-queue.test.ts` and `test/mcp/lane-consumer.test.ts`, plus this pass's own `ost_next_work` response. Observed behaviour of the product; grounds feasibility, not demand. No test was run and no result is recorded._

tests.title: A test created humans-required files an ask, so its queue entry has an age from the first pass that sees it

title: Every build that lands is announceable, including one whose only prior observation was no-spec
prose:
Feasibility belief, surfaced beside the habituation one rather than in place of it.

The candidate assumes the event it announces is available at the moment of observation. Half of that is already true in committed code and worth recording as such: `verifyInstrument` in `src/ost/instrument.ts` returns `transitioned: true` exactly when a run comes back green on a test that was `alreadyRed`. So the flip is detected today; nothing routes it anywhere. That is a smaller build than this node's prose implies.

The other half is where this could be false, and it is specific. `observedRed` matches only log lines containing `**red**`. A vacuous run files `**no-spec**`, which that pattern deliberately does not match — that exclusion is what stops a missing file minting a build permit. The consequence for *this* candidate is the opposite of the one it was designed for: a test whose only prior observation was `no-spec` goes green with `alreadyRed === false`, so `transitioned` is false and **the announcement never fires for it**.

That is not an edge case on this tree. This vault's own measurement of 2026-08-09 found 260 of 266 recorded reds read "No test files found", and every instrument this pass could write is necessarily of that kind (see the note appended to "A pass that cannot see the repository cannot set an instrument at all"). Announcing on `transitioned` alone would therefore be silent for very nearly every build this loop actually completes — a channel that reports nothing and looks healthy.

Stated so it could be false: the moment a solution is built is detectable for every solution, not only for those whose permit rested on a spec that existed.

tests.title: A green arriving after a no-spec-only history announces, and a repeat green announces nothing

title: Every channel can name a per-item source, not just a per-channel one
prose:
**Feasibility.** Ingestion already reports per channel — six lines, one each for inbox, friction, transcript, usage, atlassian and slack, saying what each captured or why it was off. The solution asks for something a level finer: each captured item naming the source inside its channel that produced it.

Stated so it can be false: some channel cannot attribute at item level. The usage channel is the obvious candidate. Its records are mechanical rollups — "108 tool invocations, p50 3ms, 3 sessions" — computed by aggregating across sessions, and an aggregate does not have a source in the way a transcript line does. If the answer for that channel is "three sessions, and this number came from all of them", then per-item attribution is either impossible there or means something different, and the solution's word "every" is doing damage.

There is a second and more damaging way it can be false, and it is already on the tree in the form of a defect: four nodes in this vault cite `TRANSCRIPT:89ac8277-29ce-4d80-827e-cefea0bebabf`, and no evidence record carries that id. So attribution today is not merely coarse, it is unchecked — a source string can name a record that does not exist and nothing refuses it at write time. A channel that names a source it cannot resolve has not attributed anything; it has written a plausible string. Naming sources and being able to resolve them are two claims, and only the second is worth anything.

That is the sharper reading of this solution and the one the test below takes: the useful property is not that each item carries a source field but that every source field resolves to a record that exists, checked when it is written rather than by a hygiene sweep afterwards.

tests.title: Refuse a source that names no record, at write time rather than at sweep time

title: Every construct the parser rejects appears in a grammar obtainable without submitting anything
prose: Readable-instead-of-discoverable-by-violation only works if the published grammar is complete and reachable in advance. Its deeper limit is stated too: writing the wrong dialect is usually a habit rather than a knowledge gap, and habits do not consult references.

tests.title: Check the accepted grammar is retrievable without submitting anything, and names every rejected construct

title: Every current consumer of the checked-in dist file can be changed to build it locally instead
prose: Feasibility belief: whatever today reads dist/ost-agent.mjs straight out of a checkout (a publish step, a deploy script, another firing) can be changed to run the build first, without breaking a path this pass doesn't have visibility into.

tests.title: Every invocation of the committed bundle is preceded by a build step, and a new consumer without one fails the census

title: Every path that can invoke the shim already carries a finite bound of its own
prose:
**Risk category: feasibility**, and a refutation retires the parent candidate outright rather than shrinking it.

**The belief, stated so it can be false:** every way the shim can be reached is already bounded by something else, so deleting its own bound cannot produce a wait that runs forever.

**Why the product's own code treats this as doubtful.** `DEFAULT_FOR_SECONDS` in `src/loop/wait.ts` is documented as "bounded rather than open-ended on purpose", with the reason spelled out: the shim exists to be written by an unattended session instead of a fixed sleep, and "a wait that can hang forever would trade eight refusals for one wedged firing." That comment is an author who already considered removing the bound and declined. This assumption is the claim that the author was wrong — or that the environment has changed — and it should be treated as the harder position, not the obvious one.

**What would make it false, concretely.** A `Bash` call composed without an explicit `timeout` and defaulting to something generous or unbounded; the shim reached from a script rather than from a tool call, where no harness clock is running at all; or a harness whose timeout kills the tool call but leaves the `sh` child alive. Any one of those is a path where the only bound was the one this candidate proposes to delete.

**Why the evidence available is not enough to settle it.** All six observed give-ups came from calls carrying `"timeout": 400000`, which is consistent with the belief — but six observations from one session are a sample of the paths that happened to be taken, not a census of the paths that exist. The belief is about the latter.

**What it does not settle.** Whether a harness kill is an acceptable *ending* even when it is a reliable one. It produces no trimmed output and no give-up line, so a bounded-but-mute wait may be a worse artifact than an unbounded-but-talkative one. That is a separate judgement, and it belongs to the branch on give-up legibility rather than here.

tests.title: Census every shim invocation path and count how many arrive with a finite bound already set

title: Every reader of source can take a list without breaking the nodes that carry a string
prose:
**The belief, stated so it can be false.** `source` has a small, enumerable set of readers, and each can be widened to a list while a node carrying a plain string keeps behaving exactly as it does now.

The readers are not hypothetical and they are not all in one place: the mapped-ness derivation in `src/processes/tree.ts`, `classifyProvenance` in `knowledge/believability.ts` — which recognises `WEB:` and `INTERVIEW:` prefixes that are *not* evidence ids and must stay honest under a list — the evidence-id-shape check `claimsStoredEvidence`, the near-miss reporter that catches `inbox:note.md` typed against `INBOX:note.md`, and the rung ceiling that caps a node by what its source channel has earned.

That last one is where the belief is most likely to be false, and it is not a plumbing problem. A rung ceiling over a *set* of sources has to answer a question that does not arise for a single source: is a node citing one `stated` record and thirty-nine `assertion` records capped at the weakest, the strongest, or something else? Every answer is defensible and one of them silently promotes nodes.

**Category:** feasibility.

**Why it is the riskiest belief under this solution.** The count saving is obvious and uncontested. What is uncertain is whether the change can be made without opening a hole in the ladder, which is the mechanism the whole tree's credibility rests on.

tests.title: Cite three ids from one node and require all three to leave the unmapped list

title: Every reader of the tree can be made to honour a retraction, and there are few enough to do it
prose: A retraction that some consumers honour and others ignore is worse than no retraction: the node is live in some counts and gone from others. This requires an exhaustive, and small, set of readers.

tests.title: Audit every consumer of the tree for whether it would honour a retraction flag

title: Every refusal the positioning names is bound to a live guard, so the copy cannot outrun the code
prose:
**The belief, stated so it can be false.** This solution sells four specific refusals — the tool "cannot mark its own output validated, cannot invent the outcome, cannot record a test result it did not watch a human run, and caps every claim at the rung its source actually earned." The position is only as good as the weakest of the four, and it depends on a property nobody has written down: that each named refusal is bound to a guard, such that removing the guard turns something red before the sentence is read by a prospect.

**Why it is the mechanical half.** The sibling assumption, "Buyers treat refusals as trustworthiness rather than as the product being worse", is a buyer's belief and is correctly a person's to measure. This one is not about buyers. It asks whether the sentences are true and stay true, and a spec answers it.

**Grounds, first-party, and the precedent that makes this concrete.** This is not a hypothetical failure mode — this repository has already had it, in the same shape and in four places at once. Until 2026-07-29, `README.md`, the Claude Code consumption guide, the unattended-pass example and the *generated* `SKILL.md` each promised some version of "the worst thing it can do is make a commit that doesn't make sense", which was false: `ost_append_to_node` could write the `## Results` heading a gate reads, and `ost_set_status("validated")` passed the invariants. The repair was `test/release/withdrawn-claims.test.ts`, which scans the operator-facing surfaces and fails if any wording of that claim returns.

That guard is the *negative* half — a retired claim may not come back. There is no positive half. Nothing binds a refusal the copy currently asserts to the guard that makes it true, so the next claim to drift does so exactly the way the last one did, and is caught the same way: by someone noticing, months later. The `docs/reference/v1-readiness.md` criteria (B1, B2, B10, P10) name the guarantees; the copy names them again in its own words; the two are joined only by whoever wrote both.

**What turns on it.** If false, the strongest available position is being built on sentences whose truth nobody re-checks — which is the one failure a position about trustworthiness cannot survive being caught in. If true, the position is the rare marketing claim a sceptic can verify by running the suite, and that is the actual product being sold.

⚠️ Unvalidated. Agent-ideated from first-party reads of `test/release/withdrawn-claims.test.ts` and `src/ost/results.ts`.

tests.title: Delete each guard behind a claimed refusal in turn and require the suite to redden every time

title: Every route a run commits by passes through a place a local hook can occupy
prose: A pre-commit hook is a guarantee only if there is no path around it. The node states its own doubt: a local hook is advisory, skippable with a flag, and absent from a fresh clone. If a run's real commit paths bypass it, the marker still reaches the commit.

tests.title: Add the hook and check whether the commit paths a run actually uses all pass through it

title: Every short category has a leaf beneath it that is genuinely under-served
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Redirecting a category to its leaves assumes the descent terminates somewhere useful. It might terminate nowhere: a category can be short of coverage while every leaf beneath it is fully served, because the category's own need is broader than the sum of its children. The descent then yields an empty list, the branch falls silent, and the pass is told there is nothing to do on a branch that has a real gap.

That is the same false negative the exemption sibling is criticised for, arriving by a longer road — so if this belief is false, this candidate loses its only advantage over the cheaper one.

**What would make it false.** A category the check considers short whose leaves are all at or above the threshold, producing an empty descent with no diagnostic.

tests.title: Descending to leaves never returns silence without a reason

title: Every source of new work in this vault can be watched as an event
prose: Nothing arriving costs nothing, which is the appeal. The failure is quiet: if some triggers cannot be watched, a woken loop sleeps through real work and looks perfectly healthy doing it — harder to notice than idling.

tests.title: Census every source of new work in this vault and check which can be watched as an event

title: Every surface that quotes a source can be made to render the sentence, not just the one that already does
prose: A guarantee that holds on one detector and not the others is not a guarantee — a reader who learns to trust the full-sentence rendering will extend that trust to surfaces that never adopted it. The property has to be universal across quoting surfaces or it is worse than absent.

tests.title: Every quoting surface renders the whole sentence, not just the detector that already does

title: Every write path can thread a session id through to its git commit without breaking tooling that parses commit messages
prose: Tagging every write with a session id only works cleanly if (a) every code path that commits a vault write has the session id available to thread through, and (b) adding it to the commit message doesn't break anything downstream that already parses those messages (changelog generation, the rollup, other tooling). If some write paths can't carry the id, the tag becomes unreliable exactly on the sessions most likely to be interrupted.

tests.title: Have someone with the vault-write code open confirm every commit path can carry a session id without breaking commit-message parsers

title: Everything the tree's claims rest on is readable without the tool, not just the claims themselves
prose:
**The belief, stated so it can be false.** The solution's pitch is that the artefact is "readable in Obsidian, greppable, diffable, reviewable in a pull request, and entirely intact if the tool disappears tomorrow." That sentence is a claim about the *whole* record — the claims and what they rest on. This node is the half nobody wrote down: that the provenance survives the tool as well as the prose does.

**Why it is the mechanical half.** The sibling assumption, "Buyers have been burned by lock-in recently enough to pay for portability", is a buyer's belief and a person is correctly the measurement for it. This one is not about buyers at all. It asks whether the artefact has the property being sold, and a directory listing answers it.

**Grounds for doubting it, first-party.** Every node in this vault carries a `source:` pointer, and in this vault those resolve into `.ost-agent/evidence/` — `INBOX_*.md`, `TRANSCRIPT_*.md` and the loop traces beside them. Obsidian does not show dot-directories: they are treated as system folders and excluded from the vault view. So on the named reader, the tree's claims are visible and the records they cite are not. Grep and git still reach them, which is why this is a narrowing rather than a refutation — but "readable in Obsidian" and "entirely intact" are the two phrases the position is sold on, and the second is doing work the first cannot support for the evidence half.

**What turns on it.** If the belief is false, the positioning is not wrong so much as over-stated, and the honest repair is cheap: either move evidence somewhere the reader shows, or say in the copy that the citations live beside the tree rather than in it. Selling continuity on an artefact whose provenance disappears in the reader you named is the specific way this position fails in front of the sceptic it was designed for — and this tree already holds a first-party instance of a claim outrunning the code, in "A claim this repo withdrew may not come back" territory.

**Boundary.** This says nothing about whether portability is worth money. That is the sibling's question and stays a person's.

⚠️ Unvalidated. Agent-ideated from a first-party read of this vault's own directory layout.

tests.title: Count how many cited sources a reader can open with the tool gone and the dot-directories hidden

title: Excluding shipped solutions removes items that are genuinely done, not items being dodged
prose: Feasibility, with a safety edge. The rule is only sound if `shipped` means built. The field is settable by an agent, and an agent that wants a queue shorter has an obvious move available — so the question is not whether the exclusion works mechanically but whether the population it removes is actually built. If any solution currently marked shipped is not, this rule hides it permanently from the one queue that would have chased it.

tests.title: Audit every shipped solution against the repository before trusting the exclusion

title: Expiry can be given its own exit status without breaking what already reads the shim's status
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

Stated so it could be false. `renderWaitShim` in `src/loop/wait.ts` ends `exit "$rc"` — the condition's own status — and at least one caller already depends on exactly that: `test/loop/wait-primitive-affordance.test.ts` asserts that a never-true condition exits with the condition's status, with `run(["exit 3", "1", "2"])` expecting `3`. Reserving a status for expiry changes a contract something reads.

The belief is that the change can be made such that expiry is distinguishable from condition-false while every *other* status the shim can return keeps its current meaning — that the only expectation that has to move is the one about expiry itself, and no caller branching on a condition's own status is silently rerouted.

It could be false in two ways worth naming: the shim may have no way to distinguish "the loop ran out of attempts" from "the last attempt returned non-zero" without an extra variable the POSIX-`sh` constraint makes awkward; and a condition that itself exits with the reserved status would become indistinguishable from expiry, re-creating the ambiguity one level down.

**What a green here does NOT settle:** whether a caller would ever read the distinction, or whether the give-up line's extra output (attempts, elapsed, output-changed) is information anyone acts on. That is usability and desirability, and no exit code answers it.

tests.title: A never-true condition exits with the reserved expiry status while a condition failing on its own merits keeps its own

title: Extent flags mostly point at real duplicates, not at distinct needs sharing a source
prose:
**Kind: feasibility (of the verdict stage doing useful work).** Stage 2 treats identical or nested evidence extents as the signature of duplicate or mis-hung concepts. The belief, stated so it can be false: most sibling pairs the arithmetic flags are really one concept wearing two titles, so the flags route judgement to merges and re-hangs rather than taxing every firing with false alarms.

**First sample, and it points the other way.** The mechanism's first output landed on the 2026-08-11 unattended sweep: twelve flags. The sweep applied Torres's interventional test to each pairing and judged all twelve DISTINCT — shared provenance without shared need. The dominant causes: one five-dimension external review record grounding five separate strategic questions (so any two of them share an extent), and single sessions that hit two different frictions in one sitting. Zero merges, zero re-hangs; twelve annotations. If that sample is representative and correct, the flag precision is 0/12 and the rules mostly convert one record with many lessons into recurring adjudication work.

**The caveat that keeps this an assumption rather than a finding:** those twelve verdicts are the pass grading its own repair tooling — exactly the self-judgement this vault's ladder exists to distrust. The test beneath puts a human's judgement on the same twelve pairings.

tests.title: A human re-judges the first twelve extent flags against Torres's test

title: Few enough consumers read a suite result as a boolean that they can all be migrated at once
prose: Changing what a result IS only works if every reader changes with it. A partial migration is worse than none: some gates would honour the exclusion set while others keep reading the same green as full coverage, and which is which becomes invisible.

tests.title: Census every consumer that reads a suite result as a pass-or-fail boolean

title: Filtering by status removes the stuck shipped solutions without hiding any that still owe an instrument
prose:
Feasibility. The belief is that `status` is a clean enough signal to filter on: every solution currently listed in `solutionsMissingInstruments` that carries `status: shipped` is genuinely built, and no solution that still owes a builder a definition of done carries that status.

Stated so it can be false: if a pass has ever set `shipped` on a solution that was not in fact shipped — or set it on the strength of documentation rather than code — then this filter silently removes real debt from the only list that tracks it, and the tree looks healthier by exactly the amount it is wrong.

There is already a reason to take that seriously. "Refuse a wiki-link that contains a newline" carries an Issues note dated 2026-08-06 recording that its shipped status was inferred from the ruleset describing the guard in the present tense, that the pass "could not confirm it against the code" because `product.repos` is unconfigured and reads of the product directory were denied, and that this is "an inference from documentation, not a verification." That is one of the five this filter would exclude.

tests.title: Seed a shipped solution with no instrument and require the work list to omit it

title: Firings rarely finish close enough together to still collide even with a serialized commit point
prose: Viability belief: moving the dist/ commit to only happen at the real merge-to-main point is enough because two firings finishing and merging around the same time is rare — if concurrent finishes are actually common, this narrows the conflict window without closing it.

title: Forcing a look before every path costs more turns than the wrong guesses did
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Requiring a look before every path-taking command costs fewer turns than the wrong guesses it prevents.

**Why it is the riskiest one.** Most guesses are right. The corpus records the failures and is silent about the far larger number of path-taking calls that worked first time — and this guard taxes every one of those to catch the minority that did not. The solution's own body concedes it is the read-before-write handshake generalised, and that handshake is this vault's single most frequent friction event at roughly twenty collisions across eleven sessions. Proposing more of the mechanism that hurts most needs a number behind it, not an argument.

**What class this is.** Feasibility and cost, answerable by replaying the corpus. Not a customer question.

**How it could come out false — and it might well.** If correct guesses outnumber wrong ones ten to one, the guard adds nine listings to save one failure and should be dropped in favour of its cheaper sibling. That would be a clean refutation and it is available for the price of a count.

tests.title: Replay the corpus to count how many correct path guesses the guard would have taxed

title: Free-form questions about the tree can be answered faithfully from the tree
prose: The value is in grounded answers with links back to nodes. The failure is fluent answers that are not grounded — which is worse than no answer, because a stakeholder cannot tell the difference and will act on it.

tests.title: Twenty-question grounding check for answer faithfulness

title: Friction shapes are separable by a mechanical signature
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Grouping assumes there is a normalisation that collapses the same refusal across sessions without collapsing different refusals into each other. The corpus makes that non-obvious in both directions. `Claude requested permissions to use mcp__ost-agent__ost_debt` and `…ost_check` and `…ost_read_repo` differ only in a tool name — strip identifiers too eagerly and three distinct withheld capabilities become one entry, and the tree loses the fact that three separate grants are missing. Keep identifiers and the paths and session ids in `File has not been read yet` variants keep 76 items at 76.

**What would make it false.** No normalisation exists that both collapses the read-before-write family across sessions and keeps the three permission refusals distinct.

tests.title: One normaliser collapses the read-before-write family and keeps three permission denials apart

title: Gate narrowings are rare enough that routing each through a person is not the bottleneck
prose: If narrowings are frequent and mostly reasonable, the person becomes the constraint — and the pressure will be to set gates loosely from the start so they never need narrowing. That is a worse outcome reached by a respectable-looking route.

tests.title: Count past gate narrowings and judge how many were reasonable

title: Git auto-init and one-command revert work on the machines this will actually run on
prose: Safety by revertibility assumes git is there or can be created, and that the worst case really is one command away. A machine where init fails, or where the revert is not a single obvious command, has none of the guarantee the design is selling.

tests.title: Test does git auto-init and one-command revert work everywhere

title: Going silent on ambiguous sources costs few enough recommendations to be affordable
prose: Silence instead of a confident half-reading is the right trade if ambiguity is rare. If most sources do not read into exactly one answer, the rule removes most recommendations and the tool stops being useful in the name of being careful.

tests.title: Count how many of this vault's recommendations would go silent under a refuse-when-unclear rule

title: Grouping ost_next_work's buckets by branch withholds no item the flat listing would have shown
prose:
Feasibility belief, surfaced beside the viability one rather than in place of it.

The sibling assumption ("The operator reads sweep-chosen work order as ordering, not as target selection") is the risk this candidate is judged on, and it is genuinely a person's answer. But the candidate's own defence of itself against the auto-select rule is a *mechanical* claim — "every bucket item is still emitted and nothing is withheld" — and nothing on the tree tests it.

That claim can be false in a way nobody would notice. The buckets are display-capped (this pass's own sweep reported `unmappedEvidence showing 25 of 377`), so grouping changes which 25 survive the cap. If grouping is applied before the cap, a branch-first ordering can push whole regions past it and the sweep would report less work than the flat listing did — which is the auto-select behaviour the ruleset forbids, arriving as a side effect of a display change rather than as a decision.

Stated so it could be false: the set of items emitted under branch grouping is identical to the set emitted flat, and only their order differs.

tests.title: The branch-grouped sweep emits the same item set as the flat sweep, only reordered

title: Having sub-opportunities is a reliable marker of being a category
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** The exemption reads one edge and concludes "category". But an ordinary leaf need can acquire a single sub-opportunity — the tree does this routinely, by splitting a need into a sharper child — and the moment it does, this rule stops asking it for solutions forever, even if neither the parent nor the child has any.

"The same refusal is rediscovered every session, because nothing carries the lesson forward" is exactly that shape today: it became a parent when its three solutions were re-parented onto a child, and it now reads as under-served for a reason that is not a gap. This rule would silence it correctly. The question is how many nodes it would silence *incorrectly*.

**What would make it false.** A node with one or more Opportunity children where neither it nor any descendant carries a solution — silenced by this rule and genuinely a gap.

tests.title: The category exemption does not silence a childless gap

title: Highlight interrupts keep their signal — the founder keeps reading them rather than tuning them out
prose: Desirability. The belief: red-to-green flip announcements arrive rarely enough, and matter enough, that the founder keeps reading and reacting to them instead of muting the channel. Stated so it could be false: the founder could tune them out within a week, the way the tree already suspects operators tune out block notifications ("An operator notified at every block keeps acting on the notifications rather than tuning them out" records the same worry for a different event class). If false, the immediate-announcement solution delivers noise, not reassurance, and the digest or criteria-note alternatives should win the comparison.

tests.title: Send flip announcements for two weeks and count which ones the founder reacts to

title: Honest accounting is worth having even though it builds nothing and moves no test
prose: A tree that reports its stall accurately and then does nothing about it for another 255 tests has converted a hidden problem into a well-documented one, and the operator whose hours do not exist is no better off. Its honest role is as a companion to a mechanism that executes, not a substitute.

tests.title: Check the rollup reports readiness and execution as separate numbers, with neither called built

title: Humans can still promote a node while the agent is structurally blocked from it
prose: Structural inability to self-certify is the guarantee. It is only shippable if the human path stays open and usable — a block that also stops people promoting has made the tree unable to record what it learns.

tests.title: Test humans can promote while the agent is blocked from validating

title: Independent judges converge on the same riskiest assumption, so agreement means something
prose: The mechanism reads agreement as corroboration. If judges scatter — each naming a different risk — then agreement when it occurs is coincidence, and a second model with no independent grounding produces the appearance of corroboration, which is more dangerous than an openly self-assessed gate.

tests.title: Have three independent judges nominate for ten solutions and see whether they agree with each other

title: Initialising only tool-created directories still covers every failure that occurred
prose: Removing the variance is cleaner than detecting it, but unconditional `git init` reaches directories the tool did not make. The narrowed rule is safe only if no scaffold target in the record sits inside an existing repository — and it still has to cover the captured failures.

tests.title: Check whether initialising only tool-created directories still covers every captured failure
