title: Inline code handed to tsx from the repo root resolves bare packages and . src paths the same way a checked-in file does
prose:
**The belief (feasibility).** A `probe` entry in `package.json` that runs `tsx -e "<code>"` with `npm run`'s cwd (the package root) lets the evaluated code import a bare dependency such as `zod` or `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and a repo path such as `./src/index.js`, with TypeScript syntax accepted, exactly as a file under `src/` or `test/` would.

**How it could be false.** `tsx -e` may evaluate as CommonJS or may not apply the TypeScript transform to eval'd input; ESM eval may resolve relative imports against a synthetic URL rather than cwd, so `./src/...` fails even though bare packages load; or `npm run probe -- '…'` may mangle the quoting badly enough that no realistic probe survives the trip. Any of these makes the sibling candidates the better fix.

**Why this is a repository question.** One spec that spawns the script and reads its exit code and stdout settles it; nobody's afternoon is needed. What the spec cannot settle is whether an agent under pressure reaches for this command instead of `/tmp` — that is behaviour across firings, not a property of the script.

⚠️ Unvalidated. Agent-ideated.

tests.title: The probe script exists and an inline import of a bare package and a . src path both load under it

title: Isolation acquits a flake and convicts a real regression
prose: The verdict carries its own attribution, which is what makes the second run worth its cost. It fails in both directions: a real regression that only shows under contention gets acquitted, and a flake that reproduces in isolation gets convicted.

tests.title: Check whether isolation correctly acquits a flake and convicts a real regression

title: Keeping the raw stream lets new questions be asked of history already collected
prose: Never discarding events is what makes summaries recomputable. The value is in questions not yet thought of — so the test is whether a week of raw events can answer things the rollup structurally cannot, rather than whether it can reproduce the rollup.

tests.title: Replay one week of raw events against five questions the rollup cannot answer

title: Killing the process at any instant leaves a state a restart can resume from
prose: Atomic writes plus an intent-and-completion journal is the claim that there is no unsafe moment. The whole guarantee lives in the instants between — a kill-at-random-points test is what distinguishes a real invariant from one that holds at the points anyone thought to check.

tests.title: Kill-at-random-points restart test

title: Knowing what was already ruled out changes what an ideation pass produces
prose: The ledger costs a read before every ideation. It pays only if ideation actually repeats itself — if a pass with the ledger produces materially different candidates than one without, rather than the same ones plus a citation.

tests.title: Paired ideation run with and without the ledger

title: Liveness is decidable for the kinds of jobs this loop actually backgrounds, not just for a local child process
prose:
**Risk category: feasibility.**

Stated so it could be false: *for the jobs this loop actually waits on, a check exists that distinguishes "still running" from "gone" reliably enough to authorise more spend on the answer.*

**Why this is the belief that decides the candidate.** The whole value of the three-valued wait is the middle value. If *still running* can only be established for a local child process — and the loop's real waits are on detached processes, work in another checkout, or a suite whose parent shell has already exited — then the mechanism returns *gone* or *unknown* exactly when a caller most needs *still running*, and a wait that says "unknown" is the two-valued wait this candidate set out to replace.

**The failure direction that matters, and it is asymmetric.** A false *gone* costs a wasted restart and is self-correcting. A false *still running* is the expensive one: it tells the caller to keep waiting on work that has already died, converting a bounded 300s loss into an unbounded one. The candidate's own prose names this — "a wait that reports *still running* by a weak check is worse than one that stays silent, because it authorises further spend on a false positive" — and it is why the bar below is about the weak direction rather than about overall accuracy.

**Grounded in what the loop actually does.** The observed session was waiting on a vitest suite writing to `/tmp/suite-baseline.txt`. That is the ordinary case here, and it is already harder than the easy one: the suite is started in the background and the waiting turn is not its parent, so there is no child to reap and liveness has to come from something other than the process tree the waiter sits in.

**What it does not cover.** Nothing about the manual half of this candidate — whether a caller-declared ceiling is one operators would actually set rather than leave at a default. That is a separate belief and no test here touches it.

tests.title: The rendered wait shim reports whether the watched job is still alive, not only the condition's exit status

title: Making a result state its gaps changes what a second reader concludes from it
prose: The field is only worth forcing if it moves belief. If a reader draws the same conclusion with and without the uncovered section, then the section is documentation rather than a guard, and the gate it was meant to inform is unchanged.

tests.title: Does a forced uncovered field change what a second reader believes

title: Many records from one self-observing actor will not inflate a node's believability
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Attaching many transcript records to one opportunity raises how well-sourced it *looks* by exactly as much as it deserves — the actor ceiling holds, so thirty self-observations read as one actor observing itself thirty times and never as thirty independent voices.

**Kind.** Feasibility, with a viability edge: what is at stake is whether the tree's headline believability numbers stay honest.

**How it could turn out false.** The rollup's per-bucket "N source(s)" figure counts sources, and nothing in that line says how many actors they came from. A solution designed to make recurrence count is a solution designed to drive that number up, and the one actor able to drive it is the agent itself. If the count and the rung are read together by a human skimming the rollup — which is exactly what the rollup is for — then a bucket showing "40 source(s), rests on assertion" invites a conclusion the sources do not support. The tree already worries about this in general ("Worry the agent is grading its own homework"); this solution is the specific mechanism that would make it easy.

**Why it is the riskiest one here.** Whether the attachment plumbing works is a small question. Whether it quietly corrupts the one number the operator uses to judge the tree at a glance is the question that decides if this solution should exist.

tests.title: Attach thirty self-observations to one node and require the rung not to move

title: Meaningful external writes are separable from churn by a rule fixed in advance
prose: Immediate in-band invalidation is only usable if it is rare and right. A watcher that fires on every build artefact and editor swap file invalidates constantly, and an agent invalidated constantly stops believing it.

tests.title: Classify every filesystem event in three real sessions as meaningful or churn

title: Most failed paths fall under a small set of nameable roots
prose: Named roots are another thing to keep current, and a root pointing somewhere wrong produces confident, uniform, wrong paths everywhere at once — worse than scattered bad guesses because it looks systematic. It only pays if a few roots cover most of the failures.

tests.title: Check how many past failed paths fall inside a small set of nameable roots

title: Most of the waits this loop actually performs are on work the firing itself started
prose:
**Risk category: feasibility** — specifically, whether the candidate's coverage is large enough to be worth building at all.

**The belief, stated so it can be false:** when this loop waits, it is usually waiting on work the same firing started, so a producer exists that could be made to announce its own completion.

**Why it could well be false, from the product's own code.** `src/loop/wait.ts` carries `WAITING_CASES`, three cases lifted verbatim from the transcripts they were refused in. Read against this belief they split badly for the candidate:

- `ci-check` — `sleep 45; gh pr checks 17 2>&1 | head`. A check running on GitHub's servers. No local producer exists to announce anything.
- `condition` — a poll on `git status` plus another session's `journal.jsonl`. Foreign state, owned by a different session.
- `started-task` — a task directory under `.claude/projects/…/subagents/workflows/`. The nearest to self-started, and even this one is a *subagent's* output directory rather than a process the firing holds a handle on.

So on the corpus as it stands the belief looks closer to one-of-three than most-of-three, and the parent solution says as much in its own giving-up paragraph. What makes this worth writing down as an assumption rather than conceding is that `WAITING_CASES` is a curated three, and the module's prose says the corpus actually holds **eight sightings**, six of them the CI-check shape. If the full eight are counted the ratio may get worse, not better — which is the answer this assumption wants and does not have.

**What turns on it.** If most waits are foreign state, this candidate is a narrow fix for a minority case and its two siblings are the load-bearing ones. If most waits are self-started, it is the only candidate that removes the ambiguity rather than reporting it better, and it should win.

**What it does not settle.** Nothing about desirability or usability. A census counts shapes; it says nothing about whether a completion-announcing producer is pleasant to write against, or whether the operator would accept losing the foreign-state cases.

tests.title: Census every blocked wait in the corpus and count how many had a producer the same firing started

title: Most of what a run stops for is independent of the answer, so it could have carried on
prose: Banking the question only helps if there is work left that does not depend on it. If the stops are mostly genuine forks — where everything downstream changes with the answer — then working around them produces output that has to be thrown away.

tests.title: Blind-judge what could have continued, before reading the answer that was given

title: Most of what this loop waits on is work the harness tracks, not shell-backgrounded jobs it started itself
prose:
**Risk category: feasibility.**

Stated so it could be false: *the waits this loop actually issues are mostly on work started through a channel the harness tracks, so replacing the poll with a completion notification would cover most of them.*

**Why this decides whether the candidate is the answer or a distraction.** Deleting the wait only works where something else announces completion. If the loop's real waiting is on jobs it backgrounded itself in a shell, nothing announces anything, and this candidate covers a sliver while leaving the expensive remainder to its siblings. The candidate's own prose names this as the first thing to check; the assumption is written out here so it can be answered rather than re-noticed.

**The available evidence points the wrong way for this candidate, and that is worth stating up front.** The one observed session — nine expiries, `TRANSCRIPT:2a686fb9-1bf7-4f01-b2f9-b66c8aea20ef` — was waiting on a vitest suite writing to `/tmp/suite-baseline.txt`, which is a shell-backgrounded job and not harness-tracked. `src/loop/wait.ts` records three more waiting cases lifted verbatim from refused calls, and their intents are polling a CI check via `gh`, listing a task's output directory, and testing a git-status condition. On that reading the assumption looks likely false. But four cases is not a census, they were selected for a different question, and the corpus that could answer it properly exists.

**Why it is still worth asking rather than assuming refuted.** A `refuted` verdict is not a null result here: it retires this candidate cheaply and redirects the branch onto the liveness sibling, which is the more expensive one to build and would otherwise be sequenced second. Establishing that early is worth more than the test costs.

**What it does not cover.** Nothing about whether a completion notification, where it does apply, is actually better than a poll — only about how much of the waiting it could reach. And nothing about mid-flight progress visibility, which the candidate gives up regardless of how this comes out.

tests.title: Classify every waiting case in the corrections corpus by whether its target was harness-tracked

title: Most opportunities the sweep calls underserved are categories whose children are already served
prose:
Feasibility, and it is the load-bearing one: subtree counting is worth building only if the phantom gaps are most of the list rather than a handful.

Stated so it can be false: if the 30 opportunities reported underserved on 2026-08-06 are mostly genuine leaves with no solutions anywhere beneath them, then this change removes a few noisy entries and leaves the real backlog untouched, and the cheaper reading is that the tree simply needs more ideation.

The count that would settle it is mechanical — for each opportunity in `underservedOpportunities`, does its subtree contain a Solution? Eyeballing the 25 shown on 2026-08-06 suggests roughly half are bucket categories carrying large subtrees, but that is an eyeball over a truncated list and is exactly the kind of estimate this assumption exists to replace.

The failure mode on the other side is quieter and is not measured by this test: a parent opportunity that carries a real need of its own, distinct from all of its children's, would be marked served by subtree counting and would stop being offered. Whether any such node exists in this tree is a separate question.

tests.title: Count how many underserved opportunities have a solution somewhere beneath them

title: Most real commands need no shell feature, so removing the shell costs little
prose: Removing the shell removes a class of quoting bug. It also removes pipelines, redirection and substitution. That trade is only good if the commands actually run rarely need those — otherwise composition gets rebuilt above the exec, badly, with new quoting rules to get wrong.

tests.title: Take the harvested commands and count how many genuinely need a shell to do their work

title: Most refusals are expressible as conditions knowable before the call
prose: Published preconditions are a second copy of the rules, and a second copy drifts. A caller checking against a stale description is confidently wrong, which is worse than being told no — so the coverage has to be high enough to justify carrying the copy at all.

tests.title: Try to express every refusal this tool can issue as a precondition, and count the ones that resist

title: Most regretted writes could have been refused by a check needing no judgement
prose: Turning the backlog of regrets into the refusal set works only for mechanically expressible regrets. The node also names the accumulating cost: invariants are permanent, and a set grown one regret at a time eventually refuses something legitimate for reasons nobody hitting it can see.

tests.title: Take the last ten regretted writes and check whether each could have been refused mechanically

title: Moving the threshold into a field gets a bound written, rather than the same prose relocated
prose: A named field the tool reads rather than finds makes an incomplete test visible from creation. The failure mode is that the field fills with the same unbounded sentence — at which point the structure improved and the commitment did not.

tests.title: Check whether the threshold field gets a bound or just the same wrapped prose

title: Naming an unfixed threshold is enough to get it fixed
prose: The mechanism blocks nothing and rewrites nothing, so its entire effect is social. If named thresholds go on sitting unfixed pass after pass, the report is an accurate census of a problem nobody is acting on.

tests.title: Do named unfixed thresholds actually get fixed

title: Naming the acceptable value does not become a way to take it without grounds
prose: Since the tool knows enough to refuse, it usually knows enough to say what would pass. But a rung refusal that names the ceiling is one keystroke from a caller declaring the ceiling reflexively — the ladder climbed by autocomplete rather than by evidence.

tests.title: Check whether naming the acceptable rung leads callers to take it without new grounds

title: Nearly every search a pass issues is a literal lookup wearing a pattern language
prose:
**Feasibility, and a scope claim rather than a technical one.** A literal-only interface eliminates this failure class only if it covers the work. If passes routinely need real pattern semantics over node text, the calls move to whatever escape hatch exists and the failures return through it, having cost a new interface on the way.

Stated so it can be false: a small minority of a pass's searches need pattern matching. It is false if passes commonly search for shapes rather than strings — headings by prefix, wikilinks by bracket structure, frontmatter fields by position. This pass did exactly that twice within an hour, matching `^\s*-?\s*\[\[` and `\[\[` to find child edges, and neither is a literal lookup.

That is uncomfortable evidence against the assumption and it should be weighed honestly rather than explained away. Two counts out of a few dozen is still a minority, but they were not incidental — finding a node's children was the single most load-bearing search of the pass, and it needed structure.

The saving distinction, if there is one: those patterns were written by hand and contained no tree text. The failures this opportunity is about all came from *interpolating* node content into a pattern. So the assumption that matters may be narrower and more defensible — that searches whose argument comes from the tree are almost always literal, while searches over document structure are almost always hand-written and safe. If the census below supports that split, the interface should be drawn along it rather than around literalness in general.

Which would make this a better solution than its current title describes, and the honest outcome of the test may be a rewrite rather than a verdict.

tests.title: Census the recorded searches and split them by whether their argument came from the tree

title: New evidence sorts after the cursor rather than before it, so a paged window never skips an arrival
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** The queue that cursor pagination would be applied to is append-ordered under its sort key — an item captured after the cursor was issued sorts after it, and so is still reachable on a later page.

**Risk category: feasibility.** It is a claim about the data, checkable without asking anybody.

**Why it is the riskiest thing this candidate rests on, and why it is probably false.** The evidence ids visible in this pass's own sweep are `TRANSCRIPT:0095203e…`, `00c3120a…`, `01e55025…` — random UUIDs, not timestamps. A UUID captured tomorrow is equally likely to sort anywhere in the existing range, so roughly half of all new arrivals would land *before* any cursor already issued and would never be served again. That is strictly worse than the frozen window this branch exists to fix: today the tail is merely unread, whereas under a cursor half of new evidence would become unreachable, and unreachable silently. The list is sorted by id and the ids carry no time, which is the whole hazard in one sentence.

**What would make it true instead.** Sorting on capture time rather than id. The sweep already reports a `mirror` block per item with a `fetchedAt` field — presently `null` for 393 of 423 records, which is its own problem — so the monotonic key the convention needs is named in the response but not populated. If it were, the assumption holds; if it stays null, this candidate should be recorded as refuted on mechanism and the tree should prefer a sibling.

**What settles it.** Read the sort key actually used for `unmappedEvidence`, and check whether a record inserted after a page was served can sort before that page's last member.

**What a verdict here does not settle.** Nothing about whether pagination is the right shape, and nothing about the other two candidates. This is one mechanism check on one candidate.

tests.title: An evidence record captured after a page is served still appears on a later page

title: No automation entrypoint invokes the built bundle without a build step of its own
prose:
Feasibility belief, and this pass's repo read suggests it is currently FALSE — which is why it is worth stating as its own node rather than leaving inside another node's prose.

If dist is committed only on per-firing branches, the shared trunk carries a stale or absent bundle between firings. That is harmless only if every consumer builds what it runs. Two do not, both read in full this pass:

- `examples/automation/build-pass.sh` sets `CLI="$OST_AGENT_DIR/dist/ost-agent.mjs"` and calls `node "$CLI"` for `build-check`, `gate`, `buildable`, `verify`, `check` and `debt`, on every firing. No build step appears anywhere before the first invocation.
- `examples/automation/github-workflow.yml` points its MCP config at `node "$SRC/dist/ost-agent.mjs"` on a fresh runner that never installs or builds this project.

Stated so it could be false: every entrypoint that runs the built bundle either builds it first or declares that a stale bundle is acceptable for its purpose.

**Why this is the assumption to build against, rather than the one to abandon the candidate over.** The gap is not fatal — it is the work. This candidate is only viable if the consumers stop depending on trunk dist, so making that true is part of building it, and a spec that holds the entrypoints to it is a definition of done a builder can act on. The failure mode it prevents is specific and quiet: `build-pass.sh` runs `build-check` *through* the very bundle whose staleness it would be reporting on, so a trunk carrying an old dist produces a firing that checks the wrong code and says nothing is wrong.

Note this is a different claim from its sibling "Nothing downstream needs dist present and current on the shared trunk between firings". That one asks what consumers *need*; this asks what they currently *do*. The first is the operator's to answer, the second is the repository's — and conflating them is why the sibling's ask has sat unanswered.

tests.title: Every automation entrypoint that runs the built bundle builds it first, and the check counts what it read

title: No call on the agent surface can mark the outcome achieved without a declared external signal
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** The circularity this solution closes can be closed by construction rather than by discipline: the outcome can carry a declared external signal, and every write path available to compute can refuse to record the outcome as met while that signal is undeclared or unmet — the same way `validated` is absent from `ost_set_status` and promotion is a human's CLI call.

It could be false. There may be no single chokepoint: if "the outcome was met" can be expressed as ordinary prose appended to the root, no refusal can catch it, and the guarantee degrades into a convention the agent is asked to honour. A declared signal may also have nowhere to live that compute cannot itself write — a signal the agent can declare is a gate the agent can open.

**Why this assumption exists as a second belief under this solution.** The solution's other assumption — "Teams can define an external signal that decides whether their outcome was met" — is about whether real teams can and will name such a signal, which is a question for people and stays with them. That belief is why this node was uninstrumentable, and it is a different claim from whether the product can hold the gate at all. A team that cannot name a signal makes this solution useless; a product that cannot enforce one makes it a promise.

**What settling this does not settle.** A green refusal proves compute cannot open the gate. It says nothing about whether any team defines a signal worth gating on, whether the signal they define measures what they think, or whether a human with CLI access uses the escape hatch every week. Those are the three ways this solution fails in the field and none of them has an exit code.

⚠️ Unvalidated. Authored by an unattended pass with no repository sight, so "this does not exist today" is inferred from the tree's own records rather than verified against the code.

tests.title: Try every agent write path to record the outcome as met, and require each one to refuse

title: No legitimate firing still needs the build agent's own Write grant on the automation-script paths
prose: Locking the build agent out of writing its own automation scripts only works if no future firing has a legitimate reason to adjust those scripts as part of finishing a real build task. If some firings do need that (e.g. fixing a broken build step they just discovered), denying the grant outright would convert a policy problem (unreviewed self-edits) into an availability problem (stuck firings) instead of solving it.

tests.title: Ask the operator whether any firing has legitimately needed to edit its own automation scripts mid-run

title: No secret ever lands in the vault or its history, and a scan can confirm it
prose: Excluding tokens from the blast radius of a compromised vault is only real if the exclusion holds everywhere — git history, a synced remote, a node body. One leaked credential in history is permanent, so the guarantee is all-or-nothing and has to be checkable.

tests.title: Test scan confirms no secret ever lands in vault or history

title: Normalization raises the similarity score of two statements of one need above the bar their raw wording fails
prose:
Feasibility assumption, and it is separable from the desirability one beside it. "A reader still recognizes their own need after normalization" asks whether the rewriting costs too much of the customer's voice — that needs readers. This asks the prior question: whether normalization does the mechanical job at all.

The parent records the measurement that motivates the whole solution — title-token Jaccard scored two names for the identical work item at **0.29**, below any usable bar. The solution's claim is that a controlled grammar (situation, struggle, desired progress) applied as a normalization step *before* comparison makes lexical comparison trustworthy. That claim is false if normalized forms of two statements of one need still score below the bar, and it is also false in the other direction if normalization pulls genuinely distinct needs together — flattening everything into the grammar's own vocabulary would raise every pair's score and buy nothing.

This is settled by code and fixtures, with no reader involved: take pairs the tree has already judged (the duplicate pairs a human confirmed, and the sibling pairs Torres's test passed) and check that normalization moves them apart rather than uniformly up. No customer interview is needed, and naming this `humansRequired` would misstate it.

Surfaced because the parent solution had only its desirability assumption on the tree, so the whole node read as human-only work when half of it is not.

tests.title: Normalized duplicate pairs clear the dedupe bar that their raw titles fail, and distinct siblings stay below it

title: Nothing downstream needs dist present and current on the shared trunk between firings
prose: Confining dist commits to per-firing branches only removes the mid-flight conflict if nothing else (a consumer, an install step, a different automation) currently reads dist directly off the shared trunk between firings. If something does, branch-only builds would leave that consumer looking at a stale or missing dist most of the time.

tests.title: Ask the operator whether anything reads dist directly off the shared trunk between firings

title: Nothing outside the build loop depends on dist being present in the committed tree between firings
prose: Removing dist/ from source control only helps if every consumer of this repo (an installer, a plugin loader, a downstream script) either runs its own build step first or doesn't need dist/ to exist between firings. If any consumer today installs or loads directly from the committed dist/, removing it breaks that consumer the moment it runs against a fresh checkout with no build step of its own.

tests.title: Ask the operator whether anything installs or loads this package straight from the committed dist without its own build step

title: One expiry period fits the real flake timeline without firing on unresolved flakes
prose: Expiry stops a workaround becoming permanent by inattention. It only works if a single period can sit after flakes get resolved and before they get forgotten — otherwise it either fires against live problems or expires too late to matter.

tests.title: Replay the recorded flake timeline to see whether any single expiry period would have helped

title: One ledger shape can carry a disposition for evidence, solutions and opportunities alike
prose:
Feasibility. The belief is that the three faces of this defect are close enough in shape to share one record: an id, a disposition, a reason, a pass. If they are, the general form costs one store and one read per bucket. If they are not, it costs a bespoke entry kind per bucket, at which point the two cheaper siblings are the better buy and this candidate should lose.

Stated so it can be false: an evidence item is identified by an ingest id and lives outside the tree; a solution is identified by a title and lives in it; an opportunity's disposition is a claim about its children rather than about itself. Those may not fit one schema without a discriminated union per case, which is the general form collapsing back into three special cases wearing one name.

tests.title: Write one disposition of each of the three kinds through a single ledger schema

title: One question is enough to get someone who knows nothing to a working vault
prose: The whole claim is that setup is a conversation rather than a wizard. If a stranger needs more than the outcome question — if they stall on where the vault goes, or what an outcome even is — then one question was the wrong size and the branch does not reach a working vault.

tests.title: Does a first-run branch actually get a stranger to a working vault

title: Operators actually read the run's completion report closely enough to notice an appended friction line
prose: This solution's own prose names the risk directly: "if operators do not actually read the completion report ... the line goes unseen." The whole value of the cheapest-to-ship option depends on that report already being read, which is an assumption about operator behavior, not something the code can settle on its own.

tests.title: Ask the operator how often they actually read the run's completion report

title: Operators actually replay a history to rebuild trust, rather than just wanting one to exist
prose: The trail's value is entirely in being read. Operators may well want the guarantee that it exists and never spend the time to walk a diff history — in which case trust is coming from somewhere else and the replayability is not what is buying it.

tests.title: Test do operators actually replay the audit trail to regain trust

title: Operators consent to a probe that looks in the places their credentials live
prose: Probing for credentials means touching where credentials are kept, and a tool that enumerates an operator's secrets to be helpful has done something they may not have wanted. Reporting why each was rejected can leak more than the rejection did.

tests.title: List what a detection probe would touch and have someone say whether they consent to each

title: Operators get real value with the vault staying entirely local
prose: Local-only confines the blast radius of any bad commit or injection to a folder under version control. It is only a viable default if the local experience is complete — if the value needs the remote, off-by-default just means everyone turns it on.

tests.title: Test do operators get value with remote push off

title: Operators will accept an agent that modifies itself while unattended
prose: Hot-swap at a safe checkpoint with automatic rollback is technically the tidiest answer. It asks the operator to accept that the thing they left running may not be the thing they left — which is exactly the anxiety the unattended branch is about.

tests.title: Would operators accept unattended self-modification

title: Operators will accept one process holding every secret, in exchange for never handing one to a run
prose: The broker's whole advantage is that the run never possesses the credential. Its cost is concentration: every secret the operator has, in one process on one machine. This solution is only worth building if operators will make that trade — and the node itself says that for some of them it is plainly unacceptable.

tests.title: Ask five operators whether they would put their secret in a broker that acts for a run

title: Operators will accept the agent living inside the vault it maintains
prose: Upgrading by git pull is only simple if committing the agent into a repository the operator keeps is acceptable to them. If it is not — and for a repository they treat as their record, it may well not be — the mechanism is elegant and unusable.

tests.title: Would an operator accept the agent living inside the vault it maintains

title: Operators will consent to shipping raw usage out of their own vault
prose: Local-first by default, full fidelity from those who opt in. The whole design chooses depth over breadth — so it is worth nothing if the opt-in rate is zero, and the question is consent to raw data specifically, not to telemetry in general.

tests.title: Will operators consent to shipping raw usage from their own vault

title: Operators will let a channel change an agent that is running while nobody is watching
prose: The mechanism requires consent to unattended change. Told plainly what the channel can do, an operator may decide that an agent which can be altered mid-run is exactly the thing they were not willing to leave alone — which would make the channel unshippable rather than merely unpopular.

tests.title: Would operators enable an update channel that can change an unattended agent

title: Operators will let a stated default stand while they are away, for a class of decision they can name
prose: Making the operator's cheapest action doing nothing requires their consent to silence-as-consent. The boundary between what may proceed on a default and what may not is the hard problem, and it is only tractable if operators name overlapping boundaries rather than five different ones.

tests.title: Ask five operators whether they would let a stated default stand while they are away

title: Operators will let their vault report outward at all
prose: Fleet experience becoming discovery input requires consent from the operators whose instances would report. This is the desirability half, and it gates everything: a mechanism nobody enables gathers nothing however well it works.

tests.title: Ask five prospective operators whether they would let their vault report outward

title: Operators would proactively check a rolling friction trend rather than needing to be pushed a per-run alert
prose: This solution reports nothing until the operator chooses to look ("it costs the operator nothing per run — there is nothing to read until they choose to look"). That is only a strength if the operator actually does look periodically; if they only ever react to something surfaced at them, a trend nobody visits is equivalent to no signal at all.

tests.title: Ask the operator whether they'd check a rolling trend view unprompted, or need it pushed like an alert

title: Operators would rather have honest gaps than guessed commands
prose:
**Kind: desirability.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** This candidate spends throughput to buy groundedness, and it assumes the operator wants that trade. They may not. Sixty-one solutions currently wait on an instrument; under this rule an unattended fleet clears none of them, and the operator's queue stops moving on the one axis they can watch it move. Someone paying for compute overnight may reasonably prefer sixty-one weak instruments they can strengthen later to sixty-one blanks and a lane.

Nobody has asked. Every argument for this node so far has been made inside the building by the party that would be gated, which is the least credible source there is for a claim about what an operator prefers.

**What would make it false.** Operators shown both outcomes choosing the throughput.

tests.title: Five operators choose between sixty-one weak instruments and sixty-one blanks

title: Ordering by time-to-kill eliminates more candidates per hour than ordering by importance
prose: The claim is that shrinking the consideration set fast beats building confidence in a favourite. It fails if the cheap disconfirmers mostly fail to disconfirm — then the queue has spent its early hours on tests that killed nothing.

tests.title: Does cheapest-disconfirmer ordering eliminate more candidates per hour spent

title: Outside teams will hand over real discovery work to a stranger running it for them
prose: The concierge model needs teams willing to give up their actual evidence and their actual decisions. A cold offer is the cheapest place to find out whether that willingness exists at all, before any of the manual work is done.

tests.title: Cold-offer test - will outside teams hand over real discovery work

title: Partitioning by actor leaves an unattended pass a reachable share and nobody's pile empty
prose: A pass that only sees its own share loses sight of what it is blocked behind — there is a real risk of a loop reporting done cheerfully while the human partition grows unread, and nothing here creates pressure to look at it. The nobody-may-act bucket is where that failure shows first.

tests.title: Partition today's sweep by actor and see whether the unattended share is reachable

title: Pointed at a vault it did not author, the checks report they could not read it rather than reporting it clean
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** The whole pitch above is "point the tool at the vault they already have and let it run the checks." That presupposes the checks *reach* a vault this tool did not author. If they cannot, the candidate does not merely underperform — it ships a grader that tells every hand-builder their tree is perfect, which is worse for them than no grader at all.

**Why this is in doubt, read off the code rather than guessed.** A hand-built Obsidian vault's notes carry no `type:` frontmatter, because nothing wrote them through this product. Three facts compose:

- `Vault.readTreeCensus` files a note with no frontmatter `type` under `skipped`, whose own definition is "enumerated, readable, but not an OST node" (`src/ost/census.ts`).
- `readTree()` returns only `nodes`. For a foreign vault that list is empty, so every invariant walks an empty set and returns zero violations.
- Zero violations over zero nodes is the exact sentence `src/ost/sweep.ts` was written to refuse: "a sweep that read nothing is a failure, not a clean run."

**The reason to think it is answerable rather than merely wrong.** The machinery already exists and is already correct — it is the wiring that is missing. `TreeCensus` carries `examined` and `skipped`, which is precisely the `offered`/`read` pair `SweepSubject` asks for, and `classifySubject` already returns `totally-blind` with `exitCode: 1` for `read === 0`. `sweep.ts`'s own docstring names the subject types it is for: "files in the directory, **nodes in the tree**, rows in the ledger." The tree-census consumer is the one named case with no spec behind it: the only wiring asserted anywhere is the search path, in `test/ost/unread-subject-propagation.test.ts`, which routes `searchSubjects(...).toSweepSubject()` into `sweepReport` and never touches the tree census.

**What makes this belief load-bearing rather than tidy.** This tree already holds the general failure as its own opportunity, "A sweep that cannot read its subject reports a clean result". This assumption is that failure pointed at the one population this candidate exists to serve — people whose vaults were never written by this tool, which is every prospect the pitch names. A grader that is silently blind on foreign vaults is not a weaker version of the product; it is a confident wrong answer delivered to strangers on first contact.

**What it deliberately does not claim.** Nothing here says the checks would produce *useful* findings on a foreign vault once they can read it. That is the sibling assumption already on this node, "Checks over a hand-built vault surface findings its owner did not already know", and it needs real vault owners. This one is the mechanical floor beneath it: the sibling cannot be true unless this one is, and this one being true does not make the sibling true.

**Provenance.** Composed by an unattended pass from first-party `ost_read_repo` reads of `src/ost/census.ts`, `src/ost/sweep.ts`, `src/ost/frontmatter.ts`, `src/ost/legacy-fallback.ts` and `test/ost/unread-subject-propagation.test.ts`, plus the `test/ost` file listing. Nothing was executed; the conclusion that no spec wires the tree census into `sweepReport` is drawn from a directory listing and the contents of the one file that does the equivalent wiring for search, so it is a strong inference rather than an exhaustive search. A reader with a shell should confirm by grepping for `toSweepSubject` and `sweepReport` callers before building.

tests.title: A vault of notes carrying no type frontmatter reads as totally blind, not as a clean check

title: Practitioners recognise their own discipline as something that has failed them
prose: The pitch describes a weakness the listener has to see as theirs. Nobody thinks they are the one who overclaims — so the framing risk, not the existence of the mechanisms, is what decides whether this lands.

tests.title: Ask ten practitioners whether their own discipline has ever failed them, before naming any mechanism

title: Provenance survives a burst, so a flood produces a backlog rather than a silent hole
prose: Degrading by slowing rather than dropping is the whole design. It fails if identity is what gets lost under load — events that arrive but can no longer say where they came from are worse than events that never arrived, because nothing reports them missing.

tests.title: Load the ingest channel at ten times observed peak and check provenance survives

title: Publishing Monitor's accepted grammar up front would cut the refusal-then-retry cost these transcripts show
prose: Desirability/usability. Assumes that if Monitor's tool description stated its constraints (no command substitution, one operation per call, working-directory-scoped reads) explicitly, a composing agent would shape a compliant command on the first attempt often enough to matter. It is possible the constraints are already discoverable from the tool description and the observed refusals reflect composing under time pressure rather than an information gap, in which case documentation would not change the retry rate.

tests.title: Ask the operator whether reading Monitor's stated constraints before composing would have changed how these two sessions wrote their commands

title: Publishing real discovery work brings strangers who try it
prose: The artefact is the marketing and costs nothing extra, since the work is happening anyway. The route has a stated expiry: publishing a real vault means publishing real evidence, which works for exactly as long as the author is the only customer.

tests.title: Publish six pieces over six weeks and count strangers who arrive and try it

title: Putting the failure first makes a human see it in a glance
prose: Reordering costs nothing and changes what is noticed. The claim is specifically about a five-second glance — if a reader still has to look for the failure, the reorder has moved a JSON spelunk to a slightly shorter one.

tests.title: Five-second status glance test after a failed run

title: Putting the uncovered statement beside the threshold changes what a reviewer does
prose: The side-by-side is a presentation change over information that already exists. It earns its place only if proximity changes the reviewer's action on the threshold — otherwise both facts were already available and both were already ignored.

tests.title: Does the side-by-side change what a reviewer does about a threshold

title: Read-only access is enough to gather the evidence the tree needs
prose: Structural inability to write back is the safety guarantee. It costs nothing only if GET-only access actually reaches the evidence — if the useful data sits behind a search or an export that needs a write, the guarantee has been bought by making the integration useless.

tests.title: Test is read-only GET access enough to gather needed evidence

title: Readers notice a degraded run without being told to look
prose: Falling back rather than stopping is only safe if the degradation is visible in the report. A fallback that quietly produces a plausible-looking run is the toolless-pass failure with better output — the thing that made it dangerous was that nobody could tell.

tests.title: Show readers a degraded run report and see whether they notice

title: Reading the whole tree at once yields reorganisations a human accepts
prose: Proposals only, with a human confirming structural change, keeps this safe. It is only useful if the proposals are good — a pass whose merges and re-parentings are mostly rejected has spent a whole-tree read to generate review work.

tests.title: One re-synthesis pass with human accept-reject

title: Real prerequisite relationships exist between the tests already in the tree
prose: Ordering falling out of a dependency graph beats ordering falling out of opinion — if the dependencies are there. A paper mapping over the existing tests either finds pairs or shows that the tree is genuinely flat and the edges would be invented.

tests.title: Paper-map prerequisite pairs among the sixty existing tests

title: Recorded decisions exist in enough volume for a sweep to find a knee rather than noise
prose: The sweep needs replayable pairs of (full input, decision actually taken) in enough volume that verdict-flip rates at each budget are signal. The vault has 134+ evidence records and every rollup is recomputable from tree history, so the raw material plausibly exists — but if the recorded decisions are too homogeneous (mostly transcript-friction crumbs of near-identical shape), the curve will be flat everywhere it was measured and the knee will sit in the unmeasured region. Stated so it could be wrong: the existing vault history contains at least enough decision diversity that the fidelity curve has a measurable knee for at least one real surface.

tests.title: Sweep recorded decisions at shrinking budgets and require a measurable knee for at least one surface

title: Refusing an unfixed threshold blocks few enough filings to be a guard rather than a wall
prose: A result recorded against 'decide a threshold before starting' cannot be refuted, and an irrefutable result is not evidence. The question is scale: if a refusal would have blocked most existing tests, it is a migration rather than a guard.

tests.title: Replay all existing tests to count how many a refusal would have blocked

title: Refusing on unknown context deletes almost no signal anyone would have used
prose: The stated cost is not missing context but a record that looks complete. Fixing the looking-complete part is only affordable if the refused records are few — and none of them a failure someone later acted on.

tests.title: Measure how much signal a refuse-on-unknown-context rule would delete

title: Refusing the colliding write leaves the tree coherent, not half-applied
prose: Detection catches the write and not the reasoning. An agent whose premise was invalidated will have most of its writes accepted and one refused — leaving a partially-applied plan built on something no longer true, which is worse than colliding cleanly or waiting.

tests.title: Interrupt a pass mid-plan with an outside write and see what state its accepted writes leave

title: Removing the repeat inference silences the loop's own closing calls and nothing that carries an error
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false:** deleting the `seenCalls` signature branch from `extractFriction` removes the two events the maintenance loop's closing step files on every pass, and removes nothing else that a reader would have wanted — because any repeat that mattered was accompanied by a result the host already flagged `is_error`, and that path is untouched.

**Risk category: feasibility.** It is a claim about what a specific edit to a specific function does to a specific input, and the repository can answer it.

**How it could turn out false.** A session can retry a call that did not error but returned something unusable — an empty result, a truthful "nothing to do" that the agent misread, a timeout the host reported as success. Those repeats carry real usability signal and no `is_error` anywhere, so they would go from filed to invisible. If the corpus holds many of them, this edit is not a filter but a deletion, and the sibling manifest candidate becomes the better answer.

**What it does not settle.** Nothing here touches whether the operator wants the quieter channel. A green on this belief proves the edit is surgical; it says nothing about whether a channel that files less is a channel anyone finds more useful, which is a desirability question for a person.

tests.title: A repeated no-argument call with no error files nothing, while a repeat whose result is an error still files

title: Rename-shaped link breaks are common enough in the histories to be worth detecting
prose: Recognising a rename as one event rather than a deletion plus a creation is only worth building if it happens. The vault histories are the record that would say so, and a handful of instances would make this machinery for a rarity.

tests.title: Audit both vault histories for rename-shaped link breaks

title: Repetition across sessions is a good enough filter for what deserves a record
prose: Making repetition the criterion suppresses one-offs cheaply and mechanically. It is wrong for the expensive single incident — something that happened once and cost a day would be counted and never filed.

tests.title: Replay the same 29 records through the recurrence rule and count what files

title: Repo sight is derivable from the surface rather than from the author
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** A flag is worth having only if the writer cannot set it. This candidate assumes the tool can determine, from its own configuration and grants, whether repo sight was available — without asking the caller. If the only available source is a parameter the agent passes, the flag records a claim rather than a fact, and an agent motivated to clear a backlog is precisely the party being asked.

The observed case makes this concrete and awkward: sight failed on this surface in two different ways on the same day — `ost_read_repo` refusing for want of `product.repos`, and the harness denying a direct filesystem read of the checkout. Only the first is visible to the tool. A pass with a configured repo but a denied filesystem grant would be marked grounded and be just as blind.

**What would make it false.** No signal available at the tool boundary distinguishes a pass that read the code from one that did not.

tests.title: The sight flag is set from the grant table and cannot be set by the caller

title: Requiring a witness path would not demote mechanisms that genuinely run
prose:
**The belief, stated so it can be false.** The solutions this tree already calls `shipped` can each name a reachable witness path, so adding the requirement documents what is true rather than demoting working mechanisms into `unvalidated`.

It is false in the obvious way: some shipped nodes describe behaviour that is real but diffuse — a refusal inside a write boundary, a redaction inside a funnel — and there is no single line anywhere that "reaches" it in the sense a path resolver could check. If a third of the shipped nodes cannot produce a witness, the rule does not tighten the tree, it corrupts a status field that was accurate.

**Category:** feasibility.

**Why it is the riskiest belief here and not the demand question.** Whether operators want a stricter `shipped` is a preference; whether the existing corpus can satisfy it is a fact about nodes that already exist, checkable today, and it decides whether the solution is buildable at all. If the answer is no, the honest version of this solution is "required going forward, existing nodes grandfathered", which is a materially different thing to build and worth knowing before anyone starts.

tests.title: Resolve a witness path for every node the tree already calls shipped and count the failures

title: Requiring difference along a named dimension raises distinctness without lowering quality
prose: Making distinctness a stated property of the set fixes the variations-on-candidate-one problem. It fails if the constraint forces candidates into shapes nobody would have proposed — trading three similar good ideas for three different weak ones.

tests.title: Does a named-dimension constraint raise distinctness without lowering candidate quality

title: Requiring the spec file to exist still leaves genuinely new behaviour expressible
prose:
**Kind: feasibility.**

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** The refusal is only defensible if an author can always name an *existing* spec whose assertions would go red for the behaviour in question. For a change inside a module that already has a spec, that is easy. For behaviour with no existing home — a new tool verb, a new lane, a new report — there may be no honest existing file to point at, and the rule then forces either a lie (pointing at an unrelated spec) or an escape hatch that swallows the rule.

**What would make it false.** A solution in the current backlog for which no existing spec file in the product suite could be made to go red without misfiling it.

tests.title: Every solution in the current backlog has an existing spec that could go red for it

title: Resetting the shared checkout to main before every firing doesn't clobber a still-running firing's in-flight work
prose:
Feasibility/safety assumption: resetting the shared checkout to main before reading which automation script to run is safe only if firings never overlap — if two firings can be in flight at once, resetting the checkout out from under a still-running one destroys its uncommitted work, which is a worse failure than the unreviewed-policy problem this solution is meant to fix.

This is answerable from the repository — check whether the scheduler can ever start a firing while a prior one is still running, and if so, whether reset is scoped in a way that can't touch it. No customer interview is needed; a human or an attended pass with repo sight should confirm before treating this as tested.

tests.title: A pre-firing reset is refused while either loop's lock is live, and runs only when neither is

title: Resetting the shared checkout to main before every firing never discards in-flight work a concurrent firing depends on
prose: Resetting to main before reading which script to run only avoids the "unreviewed policy" problem if no concurrent or overlapping firing is relying on the current, possibly-modified checkout state at that moment. If firings can overlap in time on the same shared checkout, a hard reset could destroy another firing's in-progress work rather than just its own stale script selection.

tests.title: Ask the operator whether firings on the shared checkout can ever overlap in time

title: Reverted commits and discarded branches carry the dead ends a transcript would have shown
prose: Never reading a transcript is the appeal — the artefacts are already there and already durable. It fails if the wrong turns that cost the most left no artefact behind, in which case the scan is cheap and blind to the expensive cases.

tests.title: Replay two hundred commits and count what a dead-end scan flags

title: Rolling per-shape records keep enough to rebuild the per-session findings this tree has already made
prose:
**Feasibility belief, and the one that decides whether this candidate can ship at all:** a rolling per-shape record can carry enough that every finding this tree has already drawn from per-session records could still have been drawn.

The bar is not "keeps some data". It is that the specific analyses already in the vault survive. Four of them, named so this is checkable rather than a hope:

- **"83 across 28 sessions"** — needs occurrence and distinct-session counts. A counter carries this.
- **"the worst sessions burned 9, 8, 7, 6, 6, 6 and 5 calls"** — needs the per-session *distribution*, not a total. A counter loses it.
- **"eight consecutive denials in one firing, on 2026-08-17T07:16Z"** — needs a single session isolable by id and timestamp, which is precisely what stops existing when records are keyed by shape.
- **"two captures contain a byte-identical failing command twenty-six hours apart, in two sessions with no memory of each other"** — needs two individually addressable sessions and their times.

Two of the four survive a counter and two do not, so the belief as stated is already in trouble on inspection. What would rescue it is a rolling record that keeps a per-session series rather than a scalar — at which point the honest question is whether that is meaningfully different from keeping the 385 files somewhere the queue does not look, which is a different and simpler candidate than this one.

If the belief is false, this candidate is not merely worse than its siblings — it is actively destructive, because it would delete the raw material of the tree's best-evidenced nodes in exchange for a shorter queue.

tests.title: Replay all 4 named per-session findings against rolling records and require every one to be reproducible

title: Safe-to-default prompts separate from must-stop ones by a rule someone can write down
prose: Answering on the operator's behalf is a standing grant of authority whose boundary is theirs to set. Some prompts — a destructive overwrite, a force push — must stop the run whatever the policy says, so the whole mechanism rests on that line being statable and reproducible.

tests.title: Sort the observed prompts into safe-to-default and must-stop, and see whether a rule separates them

title: Sampling between steps catches the movement before the run acts on stale content
prose:
A sentinel that samples has a blind window between samples. This solution is worth building only if real collisions are slow relative to that window — if the ground typically moves several steps before the run writes, sampling catches it; if movement and write are adjacent, sampling reports what the failed write was about to report anyway and has bought nothing.

Feasibility, and answerable from recorded sessions rather than from opinion: the transcripts hold the step ordering, so the distance between the moment a session's ground moved and the moment it first acted on stale content is a measurable quantity, not a guess.

tests.title: Replay the collision session and measure how many steps stood between the movement and the stale write

title: Seeing a path instead of a taxonomy changes which work a builder starts on
prose: The nodes are unchanged; only the rendering differs. That is worth building if the presentation moves decisions — if builders pick the same work from a route as from a hierarchy, the view is a nicer picture of the same choice.

tests.title: Does a route view change which work a builder picks up first

title: Seeing the whole sentence changes what a reader does with the fragment
prose: Rendering the elision instead of leaving it to be suspected is only worth the space if it changes behaviour. If readers act identically on the fragment with and without its sentence, the extra context is decoration around the same mistake.

tests.title: Does showing the whole sentence change what a reader does with a paste-ready command

title: Sessions update the task list as they go, not only at a clean end a backgrounded session never reaches
prose: Usability belief: an agent will actually keep marking items in-progress/done throughout a run rather than only writing the list retrospectively at the end — the whole value of this solution depends on the list being current at the exact moment a session gets interrupted, which is also the moment it's least likely to be mid-update.

title: Solo builders experience the absence of anyone to check them as a problem they feel
prose: The tool's own vault is n=1 and that one is the author, so generalising from it is precisely the move the tool exists to prevent. What they lack is friction rather than intelligence — but only if they would say so themselves, unprompted.

tests.title: Interview ten solo builders about the last decision they made with nobody to check it

title: Solutions beneath a category address the category's own need
prose:
**Kind: feasibility** (with a desirability shadow, noted below).

**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Counting a category as served because its subtree holds solutions assumes those solutions collectively cover the category. They might not. A category with five sub-opportunities, where 45 solutions sit under one of them and zero under the other four, would read as amply served while four fifths of its need has nothing.

If that shape is common in this tree, rollup does not fix the miscount — it inverts it, and the inverted version is worse because it is silent.

**What would make it false.** Any current category whose subtree solution count clears the threshold while a majority of its leaf sub-opportunities carry none.

tests.title: A category whose subtree is full stops being reported as under-served

title: Someone outside the project will run the hand arm, so the comparison is not built by its own author
prose: The operator running both arms built one of them, and there is no version of this where that bias is absent. The result is worth roughly what an outside reader thinks that bias is worth — which is why an independent hand arm is the thing that has to exist first.

tests.title: Have a second person run the hand arm, so the comparison is not built by its own author

title: Someone will pay before the tree has proved itself to them
prose: Putting a real price in the path is what turns assertion into observable money. The probe is deliberately early — a pre-order tests whether the promise sells, which is a different and harder question than whether the delivered artefact does.

tests.title: Pre-order probe - will anyone pay before the map proves itself

title: Something opening the repository will look for a pointer file without being told to
prose: The node names its own risk: a pointer nobody is required to read is a pointer that gets ignored. If cold sessions and tools do not check the root by convention, the information is present and changes nothing.

tests.title: Add the pointer file and count how many tools actually look for it unprompted

title: Spending more does not buy proportionally more worth having, so a hard stop costs little
prose: A ceiling that cannot be argued with is safe if the marginal spend was buying little. If useful output scales with spend, the ceiling is not a backstop but a cap on the work itself, and it makes the tree's freshness a function of budget rather than of need.

tests.title: Read back four weeks of spend and judge how much bought something worth having

title: Splitting proposer from judge raises trust more than a proposer's own sign-off
prose: The proposer can never sign off on its own output, which is structurally cleaner. Whether it is worth a second model depends on the judgement being genuinely different — a judge that agrees with the proposer by construction has changed the org chart and nothing else.

tests.title: Test does an independent judge raise trust over self-report

title: Status alone decides what belongs in the instrument queue
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false.** Every solution currently in `solutionsMissingInstruments` that cannot be given a red-now instrument is there because it is shipped — so filtering on `status: shipped` empties the unsatisfiable part of the queue and leaves only work a builder can act on.

**Kind.** Feasibility.

**How it could turn out false.** This pass saw 25 of 64 entries and found 5 shipped ones. If the other 39 contain solutions that are built but never marked shipped, or solutions whose behaviour is not a spec-shaped thing at all — the pricing and positioning candidates in the same list, like "Charge per assumption test designed and run to a pre-committed threshold", are the obvious case — then a status predicate removes 5 items from a queue of 64 and the operator's complaint survives almost untouched. The market-shaped entries are the strongest reason to doubt: nothing about them is shipped, and no spec file will ever settle them, so they will sit in the queue after this fix exactly as they do now.

**Why it is the riskiest one here.** The solution is cheap and obviously correct as far as it goes; the only real question is whether "as far as it goes" is a fifth of the problem or the whole thing.

tests.title: Filter the queue on shipped and count what is still unsatisfiable

title: Structure and commentary are separable from the shape of the output alone
prose: Detecting diminishing returns avoids ever defining 'done'. The whole mechanism rests on the two being distinguishable mechanically — if commentary-heavy passes look like structural ones from outside, the loop either idles while still learning or keeps paying after it stopped.

tests.title: Paper-classify the existing commit history as structure versus commentary

title: Structured dissent among diverse personas catches invalid instruments, and its catch-rate can be measured
prose:
The belief the gate-parity solution depends on, stated so it can be wrong: a debate of diverse personality-prompted judges — each charged with attacking an instrument's validity (does the spec exist, can it pass vacuously, does red mean what the question asks) and with pre-registering what its passing would commit the tree to — reliably rejects invalid instruments that a single author would wave through, AND the panel's reliability is itself measurable by machine.

The second clause is the load-bearing one. Three substrate-level ways this belief fails, named at birth: shared blind spots below the prompt layer that persona diversity cannot reach; orchestrator capture, since whoever authors the personas and aggregates the debate steers it; and dissent collapse, where inter-debater sycophancy produces a panel that never disagrees but still emits verdicts. The founder's own examples (one-distribution, one-incentive model failures expressed through every persona the substrate could wear) are the evidence these are real. Each failure mode is measurable: a canary corpus of planted-defective instruments with a measured catch rate, dissent-rate telemetry that declares a never-dissenting panel dead, frozen pre-registered pass semantics. The synthesis this assumption encodes: unmeasured self-grading is the failure case; a debate whose catch-rate is machine-witnessed is a valid counterparty.

**Natural first test (compute-only):** seed the panel with known-defective instruments — vacuous reds like the vault's own 260/266 "No test files found" episode, tautological passes, mis-scoped specs — alongside valid ones, and measure catch rate against a pre-committed threshold. Its red instrument belongs in the OST-Agent suite via the normal branch/PR flow so main stays green.

**Provenance caveat:** founder theory plus the agent's revision-under-challenge, both 2026-08-10, floor rung (`assertion`).

tests.title: Seed the dissent panel with planted-defective instruments and measure its catch rate against a pre-committed bar

title: Supporting two live ruleset versions costs few enough conditionals to stay maintainable
prose: Versioned rules multiply: every rule must keep working under every version anyone is still on, and the checking code accumulates conditionals for standards nobody has used in months. That is a cost paid forever against a disruption that happens occasionally.

tests.title: Count how many existing rules would need a conditional to support two live versions

title: Sweeps that found nothing were mostly looking at nothing at all, rather than at a subset
prose: Refusing a zero-subject sweep is worth doing if blindness is usually total. If past sweeps were mostly partly-blind — a real subject list with gaps in it — then the empty-subject case is rare and this catches the least common shape of the problem.

tests.title: Replay past sweeps to see how many were blind all the way rather than partly

title: Teams can define an external signal that decides whether their outcome was met
prose: Closing the circularity at the top of the tree requires something outside the tree to close it with. If a team cannot name a real-world metric or behaviour, the gate has no input and outcome achievement stays a judgement — just a human's rather than the agent's.

tests.title: Test can teams define a real-world outcome signal for the gate

title: Teams will pay a monthly fee for an artefact whose best months look like its worst
prose: Selling the state of the tree rather than the tool means selling maintenance. The node names the difficulty: most teams have one product and would buy one tree, and the value is least visible in exactly the months when nothing much happened — which is a hard subscription to keep.

tests.title: Offer a maintained tree at a stated monthly price to ten teams and count who asks for terms

title: The CLI fallback reaches the same vault and refuses everything the read path should not do
prose: The fallback is only a fallback if it operates on the same tree and produces the same readings. It becomes a hazard the moment it can write: a degraded pass with write access is doing unattended work through a path nobody designed for it.

tests.title: The CLI fallback reaches the same vault, and refuses the write half

title: The agent directories carry enough traffic to be a distribution channel worth packaging for
prose: Meeting people at the moment they are already deciding what to give their agent is the right moment. The directories themselves are new, their traffic unproven and their ranking opaque — so this is real packaging work spent on channels that may have no users a year out.

tests.title: List in two directories and measure installs against how far the listing was scrolled

title: The automation scripts already contain prompting commands with no non-interactive flag, so a lint would have caught the observed failure
prose:
**The belief, stated so it could be false:** the defect this solution proposes to lint for is present in the checked-in automation today, and a lint over `examples/automation/*.sh` would have refused the firing that produced the founding evidence.

**Why it could be false, and why that matters more than it looks.** If every prompting command in those scripts already carries its flag, then the prompt in session `005ca37f` came from somewhere a script lint cannot see — a command the agent composed ad hoc mid-run — and the whole solution is aimed at the wrong surface. That is not a small correction: it would mean the lint is real, correct, and irrelevant, and it would move the answer to one of the siblings, which act at run time rather than at authoring time. This is the single fact that decides whether this candidate is worth building at all, which is why it is stated as its own belief rather than assumed inside the solution's prose.

**What is already known, and what is not.** `examples/automation/` holds exactly three files (`autonomous-pass.sh`, `build-pass.sh`, `github-workflow.yml`), confirmed by a first-party listing this pass. None of the three was read line by line here, so whether any prompting command in them lacks its flag is exactly the open question — and the founding evidence's `overwrite src/cli/index.ts?` is the signature of an un-flagged `cp` or `mv`, which is suggestive and not proof of where it lived.

**Category:** feasibility.

tests.title: A lint over the automation scripts flags at least one prompting command lacking its documented non-interactive flag

title: The build loop keeps no memory across firings of which targets already failed their own instrument
prose: Feasibility assumption. This solution only adds value if no such cross-firing memory already exists — settleable by reading the loop's own source and its persisted state directory, not by asking anyone what they want.

tests.title: Ask someone with the build loop's source and persisted state open whether a per-target failure record already exists across firings
A target whose instrument stayed red after a build is skipped by the next firing

title: The build loop re-runs a candidate's instrument before spending a model pass on it
prose:
Feasibility belief, and it relocates this candidate's target from where its own prose puts it.

This node's prose closes: "distinguishing this from the sibling requires reading the build loop's own source, which this pass could not do (repo sight unavailable)." A pass with repo sight read it. The distinction the node was waiting on resolves, and neither of the two options it offered is quite right.

**Status is already re-read, so half this candidate is a no-op.** `examples/automation/build-pass.sh` puts every candidate title back through `node "$CLI" buildable "$sol" --vault .` individually before believing it — its own comment says a title that does not survive its own permit check is a parse error, not a build candidate. Nothing caches a node file.

**What is not re-checked is the thing that decides the spend.** `buildPermit`/`permitFrom` in `src/eval/buildable.ts` is pure: it reads the recorded `## Instrument Log` and never executes the command. Re-reading a node tells you what was observed, not what is true now. The module says this plainly — "A recorded observation is a fact about the past, and a permit is a claim about now" — and provides `confirmPermit` to close it, deliberately opt-in "to the caller about to spend something".

Stated so it could be false: before the build loop spends a model pass on a candidate, something re-runs that candidate's instrument and confirms the red still holds.

Evidence it is false, first-party and dated: `buildable.ts`'s own docstring records that on 2026-08-06 the loop spent a full model pass on a solution whose instrument had been green since a merge seventeen minutes earlier. That is the exact failure this node's parent opportunity is about, arriving through a route neither this candidate nor its sibling names.

**Bound on the observation.** `build-pass.sh` was read from the start through its no-build-candidates report branch; the tail was truncated by the reader's cap, so "no `confirm` invocation appears" is bounded to the portion read and is not a proof of absence. That is precisely what the test beneath this should settle.

tests.title: A candidate whose instrument turned green since it was recorded is dropped before any model pass is spent

title: The build loop selects a target from a cached list rather than re-reading its live status at commit time
prose: Feasibility assumption. This solution is only the right fix if the loop reads status once (e.g. at the start of a run or from a stale in-memory list) rather than immediately before committing to a target — settleable by reading the loop's own source.

tests.title: Ask someone with the build loop's source open whether target selection re-reads live status or works from a cached snapshot

title: The build loop's target-selection query has no status filter, or an incomplete one, letting deferred nodes back into the candidate pool
prose: Feasibility assumption. This solution is only the right fix if the loop's candidate query is genuinely missing (or misapplying) a status check — settleable by reading the loop's own source, not by asking anyone what they want.

tests.title: Ask someone with the build loop's target-selection source open whether it filters candidates on status
buildableSolutions drops a deferred solution that still carries a red instrument

title: The build prompt and gitignore alone can put probes inside the checkout, where they resolve the repo's modules and never reach a commit
prose:
**The belief (feasibility).** Naming a `.scratch/` directory in `examples/automation/build-pass.sh`'s prompt and listing it in `.gitignore` is sufficient: a TypeScript file under that directory resolves `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` from the repo's `node_modules` and `./src/...` from the repo root when run with `npx tsx`, and nothing the build loop does (`git add`, the postflight commit) can carry it into a commit.

**How it could be false.** The build loop or the model may stage with a form that bypasses `.gitignore` (`git add -f`, or an explicit path); `tsx` may resolve relative to the file's own directory in a way that breaks `./src` imports written from the repo root; or the prompt may have no natural place to say where probes go without growing the heredoc the existing spec already guards for apostrophes.

**Why this is a repository question.** Whether the prompt names the directory, whether `.gitignore` lists it, and whether a file under it loads the repo's modules are all settled by a spec over three files in this repository. Whether a session *follows* the instruction is a separate, behavioural belief this node does not carry — it needs firings, not a spec.

⚠️ Unvalidated. Agent-ideated.

tests.title: The build prompt names the in-checkout probe directory, gitignore excludes it, and a probe under it loads the repo's modules

title: The calibration workload and the measured one respond to contention the same way
prose: The ratio is stable only if load moves both numbers together. If they respond differently, the gate now fails unpredictably instead of predictably — a worse position than an absolute number, which is at least wrong in a direction people understand.

tests.title: Load the machine deliberately and check that the calibration ratio holds while the raw number does not

title: The changes an agent drafts for its own ruleset are ones a human would accept
